title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Cowboys
summary: The New Orleans Saints are 0-2 in the preseason so far and didn’t look pretty in a 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. With New Orleans entering their final preseason match, it feels vital to go into the regular season on a high note. Head coach Kellen Moore has already announced very few starters […]
full_text: Dec 23, 2012; Arlington, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys tight end Jason Witten (82) catches a pass during overtime of the game against the New Orleans Saints at Cowboys Stadium. The catch breaks the single season receptions record for a tight end in the NFL. The Saints beat the Cowboys 34-31 in overtime. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Emmons-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints are 0-2 in the preseason so far and didn’t look pretty in a 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. With New Orleans entering their final preseason match, it feels vital to go into the regular season on a high note. Head coach Kellen Moore has already announced very few starters will see playtime against the Dallas Cowboys. Despite the reserves seeing the bulk of the playing time, there’s still plenty of matchups to pay attention to on Friday night. Saints secondary vs. QB Joe Milton III Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton III has been lighting it up in the preseason. Through two games, Milton has thrown for 286 yards and 3 touchdowns with just seven incompletions. For short, the Saints defense that just allowed 254 passing yards is in for a challenge. Milton’s talent is exceptional, and he may be one of the league’s best raw talents. While he hasn’t been able to put it all together as a starter in the league, his name often comes up as a trade target for teams looking for a young passer. The Saints secondary had a strong showing against the Jacksonville Jaguars in their first preseason outing, despite the loss, but followed it up quickly with a poor performance against the Rams. With questions entering the season centered around the secondary, they’ll need a strong performance on Friday to increase confidence in the depth. Saints pass rush vs. Cowboys pass protection Part of Milton’s success has been the Dallas pass protection. Through two games, the Cowboys have only allowed one sack, with Milton himself not suffering a sack. In preseason week one, the Saints pass rush logged four sacks, with Michael Heldman recording two. But like every other facet of the game, the Saints’ pass rush was terrible against the Rams, failing to record a quarterback hit. If New Orleans wants to slow down the powerful Cowboys offense, it will come with slowing down the Dallas quarterbacks. If the Saints can replicate their success from their first outing, they will severely increase their chances of coming out on top and winning their first game of preseason. RB Kendre Miller vs. Cowboys run defense Running back Devin Neal and Ty Chandler each suffered significant injuries against the Rams. These injuries only emphasized the depletion of available backs the Saints have in the running back room. With the injuries, the Saints traded for Zamir White. Despite the trade, running back Kendre Miller is still the player with the best chance to take over for Alvin Kamara while he’s away with an injury. Through two games, the Cowboys have allowed 242 rushing yards. While facing a defense that has been vulnerable to the run, the Saints’ run game has been inconsistent. In his preseason debut against the Rams, Miller only rushed for 22 yards on six carries. While underwhelming, the fourth-year running back had plenty of plays negated by penalties and still showed the ability to create explosive plays. Friday’s matchup is a great opportunity for the young running back, who has a big opportunity to see playtime this season.

title: 5 Giants with the most on the line vs. the Jets: Does Odell Beckham need to win a spot?
summary: The New York Giants have one more preseason game left until they have to make their final cuts down to their 53-man roster. That means many players on the roster bubble have just one more opportunity to make enough of an impression to force the coaches’ hands. By the same token, there are also players […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants have one more preseason game left until they have to make their final cuts down to their 53-man roster. That means many players on the roster bubble have just one more opportunity to make enough of an impression to force the coaches’ hands. By the same token, there are also players up the depth chart who are still in competition for playing time and haven’t staked a clear claim on their role. We don’t know if the Giants will play their starters against the Jets, or how many snaps they’ll get if they do play. But the fringe starters are likely to play, and this game could help coaches decide if those players are real factors. So which five (or six) players could have the most on the line Friday night against the Jets? WR Odell Beckham Jr. The injury to Calvin Austin changes the calculus around the Giants’ wide receiver position. This is purely speculation on my part, but I do tend to agree with the initial reporting that the Giants didn’t want to sign Beckham unless it was likely that he’d make the team. I also believe that he was on the roster bubble before Austin’s injury due to the numbers game and special teams concerns. Losing Austin opened a spot on the wide receiver depth chart that seems as though it makes Beckham’s chances much more likely. In fact, playing Beckham out of the slot may even be his best alignment at this point. That said, there’s a difference between Beckham making the roster and being inactive on game day and being a real factor for the Giants. So far, Beckham has largely put good play on tape. His drop against the Miami Dolphins was bad, however he has played well away from the ball. His routes are well-run with the type of savvy and nuance we came to expect from him a decade ago, and I’m not sure I’ve ever seen him hustle to block downfield like he did against the Dolphins. That all matters, and probably matters more to coaches than any individual play. But if he wants to make the roster and be a factor, he needs to take the opportunity to prove definitively that he’s one of the Giants’ four best receivers on the field. RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. Despite a rough preseason that has seen Tracy have a brutal missed block as well as a bad fumble, I don’t believe that Tracy is in danger of being cut. However, he is in danger of tumbling down the depth chart to the point while he rebuilds trust with the coaches. Or he could find himself on the trading block. I don’t think the Giants really want to trade Tracy, however if they don’t trust Tracy and are content with a 1-2 punch of Cam Skattebo and Devin Singletary (perhaps giving way to Najee Harris), that could leave Tracy on the inactive list looking in. That, in and of itself, would be a stunning fall from grace for the only player from his draft class to eclipse 1,000 yards in each of his first two seasons. Meanwhile, the Giants could receive calls for Tracy. After all, both Jeremiyah Love and Ashton Jeanty suffered ankle injuries in the preseason that has Week 1 in doubt for them. At the same time, both the Raiders’ head coach Klint Kubiak and Cardinals HC Mike LeFleur are direct descendants of the Kyle Shanahan coaching tree. The “New West Coast” school of offense excels at attacking defenses from unexpected angles and using pass catching backs to rack up yardage. Tracy’s background as a receiver, as well as his track record of production, could make him an attractive target for teams from that school of offense. A big (and clean) game from Tracy could either re-cement his status as a primary runningback for the Giants, or boost his trade value if a needy team comes calling. DL Darius Alexander I plan on diving into Alexander’s tape in full after the Jets game. However, based on what I’ve seen so far (and I’ve watched quite a bit), I do believe the narrative being spun up around Alexander is being overblown. There is a pretty significant difference between believing a player is capable of playing better, and the player being bad. I tend to agree that Carl Banks that Alexander needs to show the Giants more, because I tend to believe that he’s capable of more. Perhaps even much more. This game won’t put paid to his career as a Giant, but Alexander does need to show continued growth, particularly as a run defender. This is the last chance he has to show the Giants that their defensive line situation isn’t so dire as to need to go on a shopping spree. It’s also true that it’s easier to build trust than rebuild it, so Alexander needs to use every opportunity to keep himself firmly at the top of the defensive line rotation. CBs Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo I’m going to cheat (What? It’s my piece and I make the rules) and do a bit of a two-fer with this one. However, I think both have a similar amount on the line — though they’re coming from different directions. On Adebo’s side of things, he’s slipped down the depth chart and needs to show that he deserves to be a starter, not just a rotational corner. Banks, meanwhile, has built a strong case for himself as a starter. He’s given great effort throughout spring practices and training camp, been sticky in coverage, and physical at the point of attack. He started with minimal opportunities, seized them, and clawed his way up the depth chart. However, things are snapping into focus with a matchup against CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens looming. Banks has been more impressive this summer, but Adebo has a much more established track record. If Banks doesn’t play against the Jets, that’ll tell us everything we need to know, but he also needs to continue to take advantage of every opportunity to build trust if he does play. Granted, it’s possible that the Giants consider Banks, Adebo, and Greg Newsome II all starting caliber players and plan to use Newsome’s inside-out versatility to match up on a game-by-game basis. However, it’s incumbent on both Banks and Adebo to inspire that kind of trust and confidence in the coaches. OC Bryan Hudson Hudson saw his stock (potentially) surge lately. That’s because Hudson still took the second-team reps at center even with Lucas Patrick healthy this past week. The best ability is availability, and Patrick has been dealing with “an old knee” (to use John Harbaugh’s description). That opened the door for Hudson, and it seems he got his foot in. If he gets the chance to play with the second team, he has the opportunity to not just make the Giants’ roster, but potentially push Patrick off the roster entirely. Hudson is primarily a center, though he also has experience at guard. That versatility could give him an edge in the battle for spots on the offensive line depth chart. I’ve also seen fans confuse Bryan Hudson with 2025 backup offensive tackle James Hudson III. They are different men, and hopefully a good game from Bryan Hudson will hopefully cement that for folks.

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants take on the New York Jets in the last preseason game of 2026. 2026 NFL season: Ranking all 32 teams’ watchability, excitement | ESPN.com 23. New York Giants. In my earnest film breakdown of sophomore quarterbacks, I called Jaxson Dart a tough watch because of his inconsistency. On this scale of Sunday entertainment, Dart is a delightful watch. His dropbacks are infrequently routine completions. More likely, you’ll get a scramble (9.5% of the time in 2025, fourth highest), a sack (8.5%, sixth highest) or a deep launch (12.4% of the time, eighth highest). Such football can produce frustrating results, but it’s fun to watch as a neutral observer. The pass rush is also fun to watch, and the Giants have a great one with Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux on the field. But the run defense might be so bad (51.7% in success rate allowed last season, 31st among league defenses) that the sack artists rarely get to shine. Remember, that was with the since-traded Dexter Lawrence II on the squad. Burns had a career-best 16.5 sacks last season — and that didn’t make the Giants any more viewable, because defense is only viewable when it gets stops. Nabers seen as a Harrison/Hill mix "I think Malik Nabers is getting open wise, Reggie Wayne. And acceleration wise, Tyreek Hill." @danorlovsky7 believes the Giants' success depends on Malik Nabers 👀 pic.twitter.com/dJ2CQioLmW — Get Up (@GetUpESPN) August 27, 2026 How this chapter of Odell Beckham Jr.’s Giants comeback story must end | The Record Somewhere between the end zone inside Hard Rock Stadium and the flight back home from Miami to New Jersey, Odell Beckham Jr. flipped the switch. It’s not as if Beckham was taking anything for granted in his quest to make the team and complete this next chapter of his improbable comeback with the New York Giants, because he almost certainly was not. This Giants offensive line is primed to be a strength the team has long lacked | New York Post After 15 years of striking out time and again in the far-and-wide search for five playable offensive linemen, the Giants suddenly are acting wealthy and shedding spare parts. The subtext to the recent trades of backup guards Daniel Faalele and Joshua Ezeudu for extra draft picks is that the Giants have justifiable preseason confidence in their five starters to be one of the strengths of the team for the first time since the 2011 team won Super Bowl 46 (as well as confidence in their remaining backups to hold down the fort in case of an injury). Francis Mauigoa blending in as the new kid on New York Giants’ O-line | USAToday.com “And me, I’m the type of guy to ask a lot of questions when I don’t know stuff,” said Mauigoa. “So, a lot of it has been helped from JMS, Jermaine, AT, and also Jon. And yeah, they welcome me in with open arms, and hopefully I can withstand the culture of the offensive linemen and improve it.” “It’s been amazing. I mean, they always help me. Whenever I missed on something, they’re always there to communicate. And they’re always telling me, ‘Alright, we got this block, we got that block.’ And even in the film room, we’re always communicating, ‘Okay, so if you want me to jump, what type of call would we call it?’ That, everything like that, and it builds chemistry.” David Bailey vs. Arvell Reese: Why Jets’ and Giants’ top picks will be forever connected | The Athletic Training camp stars. The 6-foot-4, 243-pound Reese impressed from the start in camp, consistently using speed and power to overwhelm offensive linemen and blow up plays in the backfield during his first week in West Virginia. He hasn’t really slowed down since. He’s also proven effective in pass defense, as he’s been batting away a handful of passes and tallied an interception during camp. It’s a cliché, but he already looks (and carries himself) like an NFL veteran. It might be what you expect from the No. 5 overall pick, but Reese has strung together so many impressive moments and performances throughout camp that there’s little doubt he’s ready to make a big impact his rookie season. NFL defensive rookies: Best/worst-case scenarios for 13 first-round picks in 2026 | NFL.com ILB Arvell Reese. Best-case scenario: The most naturally gifted prospect in the 2026 draft class shines throughout his debut campaign. New Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson finds effective ways to move Reese around the front seven, leading to high tackle and sack totals for the eventual Defensive Rookie of the Year. Worst-case scenario: Reese proves to be more “tweener” than linebacker, missing run fits and getting late jumps on plays due to below-average instincts and recognition. The team is left considering a position switch to edge at season’s end. Projected stats: 112 tackles, 5 tackles for loss, 5 sacks, 1 interception, 3 pass breakups. title: I hate to say it, but Bill Belichick belongs in the Hall of Fame
summary: I’m probably the last person anybody would ever expect to write an article defending Bill Belichick. I have hated him for the last two and a half decades. When I say that, I don’t mean that I have held any actual malice towards the man or hoped for genuine harm. He simply has been my […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - DECEMBER 17: Head coach Bill Belichick of the New England Patriots looks on during the second half against the Kansas City Chiefs at Gillette Stadium on December 17, 2023 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m probably the last person anybody would ever expect to write an article defending Bill Belichick. I have hated him for the last two and a half decades. When I say that, I don’t mean that I have held any actual malice towards the man or hoped for genuine harm. He simply has been my ultimate sports villain. His few and far between professional failures have been glorious for me. Belichick was supposed to become the Jets’ head coach in January 2000. The line of succession was set. Bill Parcells stepped down a day after the 1999 season ended. For years there was an understanding that Belichick would ascend to the head coaching job after that happened. Instead, Belichick resigned at what was supposed to be his introductory press conference. A few weeks later he was announced as the head coach of the New England Patriots, a bitter division rival. From there he built one of the most enduring dynasties in sports history, capturing a record six Super Bowl wins in a span of less than two decades. As the years have passed I have come to understand and even respect why Belichick passed on the Jets job at a point where the team’s ownership situation was unclear and ended with Woody Johnson buying the team. Still, Belichick could have handled the whole thing much more professionally. Scribbling out his resignation letter on a napkin? Come on. It also felt like Belichick saved unnecessary venom for the Jets. There was always a passive aggressive shot at a press conference or a deep ball late in the fourth quarter with New England leading the Jets by three or four touchdowns to rub a little extra salt into the wound. Given the Patriots’ position dominating the league and the Jets typically occupying the cellar, it felt a bit like the schoolyard bully picking on the weakest kid on the playground. A year ago at this time the eyes of the football world were fixed on Chapel Hill, North Carolina. There was a lot of intrigue about how Belichick would do moving to the college game and taking over as the head coach of the University of North Carolina’s football team. As the Tar Heels begin a new season tomorrow, I think it is fair to say the program and Belichick have plenty of eyes on them once again. This year, though, it is born out of a grisly curiosity. The Belichick Era at North Carolina veered badly off course from the start, an embarrassing 48-14 loss at home to TCU. The team stumbled to an ugly 4-8 season. The football was bad. The headlines were worse. From Jordon Hudson to Mike Lombardi the North Carolina football program has become as notable for its off field dysfunction as for its on field failures. At this point the biggest question around the program is precisely when UNC will pull the plug on this disaster, and how bad it will get before that happens. Note that I said, “when,” not, “if.” As if all of this wasn’t enough, Belichick suffered another embarrassment in January as the selection committee of the Pro Football Hall of Fame declined to enshrine him in his first year of eligibility. The only sign of Belichick during induction weekend in July was a joke his former kicker Adam Vinatieri made at his expense. 🚨🚨INSANE🚨🚨 ADAM VINATIERI TOOK SHOTS AT BILL BELICHICK DURING HIS EPIC HALL OF FAME SPEECH. “UNFORTUNATELY, BILL COULDN’T BE HERE RIGHT NOW… IT’S BECAUSE HE’S JUDGING HIS GIRLFRIEND’S CHEERLEADING COMPETITION” 💀💀💀 pic.twitter.com/QLNQOIWSWr — MLFootball (@MLFootball) August 8, 2026 This is where I have to draw the line. I am a Jets fan, yes. I am also passionate about the history of the game. When I was a kid my dad instilled in me that to appreciate the sport as a fan, you have to understand its history. The past explains how we got here. I cringe whenever I log onto social media these days because inevitably I will see some graphic ranking the “greatest of all-time” at a position. Inevitably the list would make you believe NFL history began in the year 2000. Occasionally one of the lists will at least trace back to players from the 1980s. Once in a blue moon, it will include the entire Super Bowl era. But there are so many greats that fans never learn about. For whatever reason, this problem is more pronounced in football than any other sport. We don’t treat the history of the game with reverence. The average baseball fan has heard of Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth, and Ted Williams. The average basketball fan has heard of Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain. How many football fans don’t know Sammy Baugh, Bronko Nagurski, Don Hutson, Raymond Berry, Chuck Bednarik, and so many other all-time greats who played before the Super Bowl era? We owe the game we enjoy to the contributions these players made to the sport. Yet they are lost to history. So I think about fans in the future. I ask myself whether there’s a reasonable way to justify the coach who has the most Super Bowl wins, is tied for the most overall NFL championships, and has the second most wins not being in the Hall of Fame. The answer is a clear no for me. Many fans don’t agree with that. They argue Belichick was a vastly overrated coach. I think there are five reasons people make this argument. Belichick was at the center of a massive cheating scandal that tarnished his image. When he left the Patriots, the franchise was a mess. Within two years of his departure, they were rebuilt into a Super Bowl team. Tom Brady departed New England and immediately won a championship with another team. As this happened, the Patriots under Belichick slowly sunk to the bottom of the league. This suggests that Belichick was along for the ride after lucking his way into having arguably the greatest quarterback of all-time. The end of Belichick’s career has been hideous. Not only did the Patriots sink to the bottom of the NFL after Brady left. We have the current fiasco at North Carolina. People just don’t like Belichick and revel in any chance to knock his legacy and call him a fraud. If you are in the fifth category, I understand where you are coming from. However, I will warn you right here that if you won’t listen to any arguments that Belichick was a great coach, this article won’t be for you. I harbor no hard feelings if you want to leave right now and check out something else on this site. For those of you who are willing to engage with a nuanced discussion on the greatest of a complex figure, please join me below. I fully intend to address each of the five arguments against Belichick’s greatness before we finish. First, however, I think it’s important to establish what actually made him great. Great coaches come in all shapes and sizes. It always makes me chuckle a bit when a team is conducting a coaching hire, and fans state that inherently an offensive coach is greater than a defensive coach or that running a particular scheme is important. At the end of the day, no two coaches are alike. All bring something different to the table. As for Bill Belichick, there are the five things I would argue that set him apart. Belichick was the greatest defensive mind of his era. As time passes our memories fade. We have a way of jumbling things in our mind to fit convenient narratives. When it comes to the Patriots dynasty, we tend to think about the end years when Tom Brady was an unstoppable force. It wasn’t always that way, though. New England was a balanced team through its first three Super Bowl wins. Tom Brady wasn’t yet TOM BRADY . Now don’t get me wrong. He was still an elite quarterback in this era, arguably still the best in the league. But rather than serving as a wrecking ball to defenses for 60 minutes, his game was more defined by playing efficient football and then delivering the clutch fourth quarter drive to win the game. Brady…

title: Scouting Jets cornerback Keenan Garber
summary: The Jets recently signed cornerback Keenan Garber, who has already played one game for the Jets in preseason. Today, we break Garber down in detail. The 26-year old Garber is listed at 6’0” and 188 pounds and was undrafted out of Kansas State last season. He has yet to make his NFL debut but started […]
full_text: Dec 26, 2024; Phoenix, AZ, USA; Kansas State Wildcats cornerback Keenan Garber (1) against the Rutgers Scarlet Knights during the Rate Bowl at Chase Field. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Jets recently signed cornerback Keenan Garber, who has already played one game for the Jets in preseason. Today, we break Garber down in detail. The 26-year old Garber is listed at 6’0” and 188 pounds and was undrafted out of Kansas State last season. He has yet to make his NFL debut but started 17 games in college, during which he recorded 52 tackles, nine pass breakups and two interceptions. Background Garber was a three-star high school recruit, who originally headed to Kansas State as a wide receiver in 2019. In his first three seasons, he played in 19 games, during which he registered 88 yards on nine touches. That included a 54-yard reception. In 2022, Garber remained as a wide receiver, but wasn’t getting any opportunities, so he opted to transfer to defensive back. An injury crisis during the Big 12 title game meant he was called into action, making one tackle. That was his only statistical contribution in 14 games that season. Garber opted to remain at cornerback for his redshirt season, then remained there for another year, as he had an extra season of eligibility due to the pandemic. During those two seasons, he started 17 of 26 games and recorded 52 tackles, nine pass breakups, 1.5 tackles for loss and two interceptions, including a pick-six. Despite a solid pro day workout, Garber was not considered as likely to be drafted and ultimately signed as an undrafted free agent with the Vikings, for whom he attended training camp and played in three preseason games. After final cuts, he had brief stints on the practice squad for the Colts and Lions, but didn’t get elevated for a regular season game. The Jets signed Garber just over a week ago, but he already led them in defensive snaps in his first appearance with them in preseason. He had three tackles in that game having registered no stats in three preseason appearances with Minnesota. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Garber brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Garber has average size, but lacks ideal length. However, he is a good athlete. At his pro day, he ran a 4.50 in the 40-yard dash and managed 18 bench press reps with good agility and explosiveness numbers. Usage Garber has played almost exclusively as an outside cornerback in college and preseason action. When he was a wide receiver, he also played exclusively outside. Coverage Garber’s coverage numbers in his first season as a full-time cornerback were solid as he only allowed a catch on 50 percent of his targets for an average of less than 12 yards per catch. However, his numbers were worse in his final season as he gave up a 67 percent catch rate and almost 15 yards per catch. He’s still relatively new to the position, although he did play defensive back in high school, but Garber moves around relatively smoothly. However, he can be late to react to route breaks. Tet McMillan was a good test for him in his first season as a full-time cornerback, but he gave up five catches for 80 yards as McMillan went 11-for-138 in total. At times, you’re left wondering if Garber completely trusts his own abilities because he often seems to play too far off his receiver. Over the two seasons, Garber gave up three touchdowns. The longest play he gave up was only 45 yards but he gave up four plays of over 35 yards in his final season. Generally, he hasn’t been someone who has let receivers get behind him on deep throws, though. Ball Skills With nine passes defensed and two interceptions, including a pick-six, Garber has flashed some abilities to make plays on the ball with good timing and the ability to knock the ball out before a receiver can secure the catch. Garber was only targeted 11 times in four seasons but didn’t have a dropped pass as a wide receiver. However, he doesn’t have a big catch radius to get his hands on the ball. Tackling Garber only had six missed tackles in each of his seasons as a full-time cornerback but he wasn’t a particularly productive tackler so his missed tackle rate was higher than you’d ideally like to see. Even on plays he makes, he displays rawness as a tackler, often diving in low or throwing a shoulder recklessly at the ball carrier. He did not force any fumbles in his college career. Run Defense Garber has been rated as below average in run defense on analysis sites such as Pro Football Focus. Since he played on the outside, he barely contributed in this role. In his two seasons as a full-time cornerback he had eight tackles and six missed tackles in the running game. Only two of those tackles were near the line of scrimmage. Blitzing It was extremely rare for Garber to blitz from the outside cornerback position and he didn’t register a sack in his college career, although he did have one pressure. Special Teams Garber was on the field goal defense and saw some time as a vice and as a punt gunner in college, but didn’t have a great deal of production as he had just one special teams tackle. He did have one highlight, though, returning this extra point 91 yards for a score. Physicality Garber only had seven penalties in his college career but was called for defensive pass interference twice and defensive holding once in 2024. He can also be outmuscled at the catch point from time to time. Instincts Playing on the other side of the ball may have helped Garber in terms of being able to read offensive formations or anticipate the receiver’s routes. He also displayed good play recognition on the best play from his Jets debut, as he reacted well for this stop in the flat. He was an academic all-Big 12 selection in 2024. Attitude/Demeanor Garber showed a good team-first attitude when he converted from wide receiver to cornerback. No doubt frustrated at not getting any opportunities on offense, it was Garber himself who approached coaches with the idea of converting. Injuries Injuries haven’t affected Garber during his collegiate career. He played in 59 games in total, including 58 over his last five years. Scheme Fit As noted, Garber is an outside cornerback, and that’s where he played – with the third unit – in his preseason debut. He may be considered more of a developmental piece though. He was a teammate of current Jets safety VJ Payne at Kansas State. Conclusions Garber acquitted himself well enough in his first preseason appearance but the Jets have a few cornerbacks not currently playing who are clearly going to be on the final roster so there is no realistic chance of him making the team. If he has another solid performance against the Giants, then perhaps Garber will have convinced the coaching staff that he’s got some potential and could continue to develop on the practice squad or if he is re-signed before camp next season. The latter option, giving him a chance to play in the UFL this spring, could be a viable path to getting back into camp with the Jets or another team a year from now.

title: Nate Lynn: More Than Your Typical Camp Standout?
summary: Anyone who has followed the Jets at any sort of detailed level over the years knows they have seen their fair share of preseason standouts. For the most part, these players don’t work out. For every Wayne Chrebet, there have been countless guys who Jets fans have gotten excited about, only for them to never […]
full_text: Aug 21, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; New York Jets defensive tend Nate Lynn celebrates with New York Jets defensive end Paschal Ekeji (54) after sacking Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Drew Allar during the fourth quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Anyone who has followed the Jets at any sort of detailed level over the years knows they have seen their fair share of preseason standouts. For the most part, these players don’t work out. For every Wayne Chrebet, there have been countless guys who Jets fans have gotten excited about, only for them to never make much of an impact at the NFL level. Zach Sudfeld, Rontez Miles, Chris Streveler, Ryan Spadola, Clyde Gates…well, you get the point. Preseason normally doesn’t tell us much, and unfortunately, beating up on a bunch of backups and fringe roster players doesn’t necessarily translate to making valuable contributions during the regular season. However, what if I told you there was a player on the 2026 Jets who might actually be able to make an impact going forward because of his intriguing profile and history? Listen, listen. I know how this sounds. I just gave you a complete warning about why you cannot delude yourself into buying into positive preseason performances. I’m always reminded of Tobias Fünke’s hilarious line from Arrested Development whenever I start talking myself into one of these guys: That pretty much sums it up. It never works. Or, at least, it hardly ever works in NFL terms. But as fans, we delude ourselves into thinking there’s a chance. This year, my guy is Nate Lynn. Lynn is a recent acquisition who stood out in the Jets’ preseason opener last week. And while it would be incredibly premature to suggest he’s going to become some sort of impact player (or even make the team), there are enough things about his background and profile to make me at least a little more interested than I normally would be in a preseason standout. Let’s take a look at Lynn’s history and why there might be something here. Background Lynn is a 24-year-old edge rusher entering his third season in the NFL. He originally came into the league as an undrafted free agent in 2024 after a strong collegiate career at William & Mary. Known for his versatility, Lynn played all over the defensive line in college, often moving inside despite weighing around 255 pounds. That versatility was a big part of what made him interesting. He had impressive speed for someone who spent so much time lined up around the B-gap, although his testing numbers were much more modest when viewed strictly through the lens of a stand-up edge rusher. Still, Lynn evidently did enough to impress then-Lions general manager Brad Holmes and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn. After a solid offseason and training camp, Lynn’s rookie season was unfortunately cut short in his very first preseason game against the Giants. He suffered a torn ligament in his shoulder, which was particularly discouraging considering he had already flashed with a sack in the game. Lynn spent the entire 2024 season on injured reserve. Then came 2025. Once again, Lynn generated buzz throughout the offseason, with Brad Holmes publicly describing him as “impressive.” And his preseason performance backed that up. In four preseason games (the Lions played in the Hall of Fame Game) Lynn accumulated 10 total pressures and a sack. Those 10 pressures ranked among the top three of all edge rushers that preseason, while his PFF grade and pass-rush win rate were both in the 99th percentile among qualified pass rushers. Despite all of that, Lynn was cut. That came as somewhat of a surprise. A quick look at the Lions 53-man roster projections from beat writers that summer shows that Lynn was generally expected to make the team. The overall sentiment seemed to be that he had done enough to stick around. Instead, he ended up signing with the Titans’ practice squad. Then came another regime change, and Robert Saleh ultimately opted not to keep him around. That brings us to the Jets. So, What Do We Make of Him? Lynn has played just one preseason game with the Jets, but he immediately looked like one of the best players on the field, even if he was doing it against backups. He finished with two sacks against the Steelers and was the Jets’ second-highest graded defensive player in the game. One of those sacks came against Steelers starting tackle Broderick Jones. Obviously, none of this means Lynn is suddenly going to become a star. If anything, he might still be more likely not to make the Jets’ 53-man roster. That’s the reality of being an undersized, relatively unproven edge rusher who has bounced around the league. The intriguing part though, is Lynn has now produced in essentially every preseason setting in which he’s been given an opportunity. In 2025, he was one of the most productive pass rushers in the entire preseason and still couldn’t crack the Lions’ roster. Now, a year later, he has joined another team and immediately flashed again. Maybe this is just another case of a guy dominating against players who won’t be on NFL rosters in a few weeks. There are certainly plenty of reasons to believe that. But unlike some of the classic Jets preseason stars we’ve fallen in love with over the years, Lynn at least has a track record that makes me a little more interested. He has collegiate production, legitimate versatility, and he has already flashed on multiple occasions in preseasons. Now he has one more preseason game to make his case. He’s got a lot to play for tonight. And I’ll be rooting for him.

title: 10 fascinating Eagles questions as training camp ends
summary: Fantasy football drafts have been set. The preseason games are almost over. Training camp is done. Yep, the 2026 NFL season is nearly here, and your Philadelphia Eagles are once again a contender. Are they the favorites to get back to the Super Bowl and/or win it? Nope. But that’s OK. It’s always better to […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 15: Jihaad Campbell #11 of the Philadelphia Eagles lines up before the snap during an NFL preseason football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fantasy football drafts have been set. The preseason games are almost over. Training camp is done. Yep, the 2026 NFL season is nearly here, and your Philadelphia Eagles are once again a contender. Are they the favorites to get back to the Super Bowl and/or win it? Nope. But that’s OK. It’s always better to fly under the radar. We do know that this Eagles roster is stacked with really good players, particularly on the defensive side of the ball, featuring a potential top-five unit. Offensively, there are questions, and there will be struggles. But it was time for this scheme to evolve, so it’s fun anticipating what it all may look like once the regular season begins. Still, there are a number of questions as yet unanswered as training camp winds down. Here are 10 of the more fascinating ones. 1) Who is the backup QB? Or perhaps an even more fascinating question… “Is the Eagles’ backup QB for 2026 currently on the roster?” The “battle” between incumbent No. 2 Tanner McKee and veteran ginger Andy Dalton has not been a scintillating one. Dalton appeared to be getting more run as Jalen Hurts’ backup this summer, but McKee appeared to outplay him during his more limited action. Neither QB bathed themselves in glory though, and given the fact Dalton appeared to be the front-runner for most of training camp, it’s fair to wonder how much faith the organization has lost in McKee following his lackluster performance in Week 18 last season. In an ideal scenario, one of these players will be traded after the team’s final preseason game. I would keep McKee over Dalton. There’s more upside there. But if Howie Roseman doesn’t feel good about either player, perhaps a long-rumored trade for Minnesota’s J.J. McCarthy or Indianapolis’ Anthony Richardson will come to fruition. 2) Can Saquon Barkley lead your fantasy team’s RBs? Last year, I picked Barkley No. 2 overall in my fantasy draft. I finished in 11th place in a 12-team league. The two were related. No one expected Barkley to repeat his 2,005 yard performance from 2024, but a drop from 125.3 yards per game to 71.3 wasn’t on anyone’s bingo card. The offensive line was banged up all year and the playcalling and scheme did no one any favors, either. So we’re all curious to see how Barkley will do in a Sean Mannion offense with a healthy offensive line. If you draft Barkley as your RB1, are you doomed to failure like I was a year ago? 3) Which receiver finishes with the 2nd-most yards? Barring a disaster (or a breakout performance, I suppose), DeVonta Smith is going to be this team’s leader in receiving yards. But who will be No. 2? The Ringer’s Philly Special spent the last couple of podcasts asking this question and it made me want to weigh in, too. Based on the preseason, it would appear Dontayvion Wicks is the most likely answer. He looked elusive and quick and is familiar with Mannion and what he’s likely to do. He’s also likely to get a lot of snaps, probably as the team’s slot receiver to start. Makai Lemon will enter the season as the No. 2, but he missed most of the summer with a hamstring injury. Will he be able to ramp it up and develop enough chemistry with Hurts in a short amount of time to emerge as the team’s second-leading receiver? Rookie receivers rarely have that kind of immediate immpact. And what about camp superstar Darius Cooper? Is he capable of making a “leap?” And don’t forget tight end Dallas Goedert, who made 15 starts for the first time in his NFL career a season ago, finishing with 591 yards and a career-high 11 TDs. How will Mannion’s offense affect his productivity? Health will be a major factor. My money is on Wicks. 4) How many starts does Markel Bell make? The rookie third-round pick has been one of the most impressive new players in camp this year and it sure does look like the team has found its eventual Lane Johnson replacement. For 2026, he’ll enter the season as the team’s swing tackle, and while I’m optimistic about the health of Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata, I say that every year. And every year, one of the tackles misses time. I think we have to pencil Bell in for at least two starts at one of the tackle spots, and if Johnson or Mailata is out for longer, he’s going to be the guy to get those reps, not veteran Fred Johnson. I’m excited to see more of Bell, but hopefully it doesn’t come this year at the expense of either of the team’s Pro Bowl offensive tackles. 5) Is the Eagles’ No. 2 TE currently on the roster? Goedert will be the starter, but he’s also an injury-prone, 31-year-old tight end. The team drafted Eli Stowers in the second round of the draft hoping he’d be TE2, but his well-documented summer struggles have torpedoed those chances. Right now, run-blocking specialist Johnny Mundt is the No. 2, and if Goedert were to go down, there would be absolutely zero pass-catching options at the tight end position. In a recent Philly Voice post , Jimmy Kempski noted the Rams appear to have a few too many tight ends on the roster and that one of them could be had in a trade, with Davis Allen mentioned as the most obvious candidate. Earlier in the off-season, former Eagle-turned-Cardinal-turned-Commander Zach Ertz expressed a desire to return to Philadelphia. He has recovered from a devastating knee injury at the end of 2024 and believes he can still play. Other names in the ether, more likely to be dealt at the trade deadline, are Carolina’s Ja’Tavion Sanders, Denver’s Evan Engram and Atlanta’s Kyle Pitts. 6) When will Jonathan Greenard be back? The Eagles’ biggest off-season acquisition has missed the entire summer with a pec injury that landed him on the PUP list, and NFL insider Adam Schefter said this week he’s unlikely to play in Week 1. ESPN's @AdamSchefter Doesn't Think Jonathan Greenard Will Play Week 1 #FlyEaglesFly | @asalciunas975 🎙️ 📸 Mitchell Leff/Getty Images pic.twitter.com/Mi5pA7488R — 97.5 The Fanatic (@975TheFanatic) August 26, 2026 Thankfully, the Eagles are pretty deep on the defensive line, but edge rusher was an area of uncertainty as the off-season began and, without Greenard, they’re lacking one big pass rusher. Also, how long will it take Greenard to get into game shape and perform at his normal levels of production when he does return? Greenard should not return until he’s fully healthy, even if he misses the first month. No one wants him to come back too soon and play at a sub-optimal level, like we saw with Cam Jurgens and Landon Dickerson a year ago. 7) Who will lead the Eagles in sacks? Jalyx Hunt had perhaps the best training camp of anyone on the roster and, with Greenard hurting, he could be the guy. But he’s not the only candidate. Nolan Smith is finally healthy to start the season and is looking to have a big campaign in the final year of his rookie deal. And on the inside, Jalen Carter, with a big-money contract extension tucked under his very large arms, looks exceedingly good right now, too. It’s harder for tackles to pile up as many sacks as edge rushers, but Carter’s immense talent automatically makes him a possible exception to that rule. My money is on Hunt, with Greenard piling up some sacks late in the season once he returns. 8) Are we sleeping on Jihaad Campbell? The talk this summer has been centered on the emergence of Jeremiah Trotter, Jr. as a starting-caliber linebacker in the NFL. That’s a wonderful development and a fantastic legacy story, but are we sleeping on Campbell? Remember, Campbell was a first round pick and had all the hype in the world at this time last year. Opposing players were cursing that the Eagles had landed a player with the kind of potential impact Campbell has. He understandably moved to the bench last season when…

It’ll be interesting to see how he fares. No Eli Stowers The rookie tight end is dealing with a hamstring injury. It’s a shame we won’t get to see him in this setting. What is going to happen with these rookie safeties? The Eagles have gotten some promising play from two rookie safeties: Kapena Gushiken and Maximus Pulley. Besides having kickass names, they’re both playing really well all over the Eagles secondary. Safety is probably the most precarious position on the roster, so another strong game from both first years could land them a roster spot and maybe some snaps early in their careers. The international players The Eagles have two defensive linemen who are playing their first minutes of football ever this summer. Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru came into camp with a lot of talent and no football experience to speak of. Both players have shown flashes through two weeks of preseason. Can both of these guys make the roster when the defensive line group is so deep? It’s hard to imagine, but they will both be playing hard tonight to prove they deserve a spot.

Graham previously expressed in playing one more season but he also said he’d like to participate in training camp, which ended earlier this week. So, we’ll just have to wait and see on this front. In the meantime, what we DO know is that Graham is joining the PHLY Eagles gameday crew : 🚨 Introducing our 2026 @PHLY_Eagles Gameday Crew We’re bringing you pre- and postgame coverage all season long with: – @Bo_Wulf – @EJSmith94 – @FDuffyNFL – @brandongraham55 – @RealTaIkWithMJ1 – @BrandonGowton pic.twitter.com/uAQ47AnfOp — PHLY Sports (@PHLY_Sports) August 27, 2026 It’ll be good to hear Brandon Lee Graham’s insight on the Birds this year both in the form of weekly gameday coverage and the second season of his Unblocked podcast . title: Eagles News: Time to bring Zach Ertz back?
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Roob’s Observations: Can Howie Roseman keep Uar Bernard and Josh Weru on the 53? – NBCSPWOULD HOWIE CONSIDER BRINGING BACK THIS FORMER EAGLE? We know Howie Roseman loves bringing former Eagles back to Philly. He does it all the time (Marcus Epps, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Vinny […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 26: Zach Ertz #86 of the Washington Commanders leaps with the football during the fourth quarter in the NFC Championship Game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 26, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Roob’s Observations: Can Howie Roseman keep Uar Bernard and Josh Weru on the 53? – NBCSP WOULD HOWIE CONSIDER BRINGING BACK THIS FORMER EAGLE? We know Howie Roseman loves bringing former Eagles back to Philly. He does it all the time (Marcus Epps, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Vinny Curry, Nick Foles, Jordan Howard, DeSean Jackson, Jordan Matthews, many others). We also know that with Eli Stowers struggling this preseason Roseman could be in the market for a second receiving tight end who could be an upgrade over Grant Calcaterra or E.J. Jenkins. Here’s an idea: Zach Ertz. Ertz is reportedly healthy after tearing his right ACL in the Commanders’ loss to the Vikings in Minneapolis last December. Ertz is 35, but he can still play. We saw him catch 11 balls for 104 yards in the 2024 NFC Championship Game and last year before he got hurt he was in the top 10 among all tight ends in catches and yards and on pace for 65 catches and 659 yards. He played with Jalen Hurts in 2020 and the first half of 2021, before he was traded to Arizona, so he’s got some chemistry with the quarterback. Ertz has made over $80 million in his 13-year career, so he won’t be looking for a big payday. He’s a class act and still has strong ties with Philly through his Ertz Family Foundation. One side note to this: Ertz is fifth all-time among tight ends with 825 catches and only needs 11 receptions to break Harold Carmichael’s franchise record of 589 receptions, and when he was traded back in 2021 he said he’d love to come back one day and finish his career here. Probably unlikely but ya never know. Eagles 53-man roster prediction: How tough decisions at wide receiver, tight end and D-line will shake out – Inquirer Tight end has overtaken safety as the most likely area Roseman might address via trade or by some other means. The Eagles were probably expecting Stowers to need time, especially when it came to blocking. But he rarely practiced with Hurts, if at all, and recently suffered a setback with his hamstring. Redshirting the second-rounder would set off alarms, so it’s unlikely Roseman takes that route. But a swap — or signing a veteran like Zach Ertz off the street — would also speak volumes. Goedert is still a competent “Y” receiver, while Mundt will shoulder some of the “F” blocking responsibilities. But tight ends often need to be dual-purpose within Sean Mannion’s new Kyle Shanahan-style scheme and neither is as competent in the opposite discipline. If Stowers isn’t healthy by the opener, or is unable to contribute on special teams in the early going, Latu seems the likely fourth option. He can also fill the fullback role if Mannion adds that wrinkle to the offense. The first “per sources” in the history of the @LockedOnBirds squad show dropped today by @MarcFarzetta 👀 Zach Ertz would love to return to the #Eagles in 2026 and thought it was likely not happening when they drafted Eli Stowers Could it happen now that Stowers is struggling? https://t.co/hpGjrqUIGJ pic.twitter.com/RTdLdmrxBI — Louie DiBiase (@DiBiaseLOE) August 27, 2026 Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Some hints for the final preseason game? – BGN Wednesday marked the seventeenth and final Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! PHLY Adds Two-Time Super Bowl Champion Brandon Graham Back To Roster Ahead Of 2026 Season – Barrett Media What We Know: Brandon Graham will appear regularly on PHLY’s Eagles postgame coverage. The Super Bowl-winning defensive end retired after a 15-year Eagles career defined by his signature strip-sack in Super Bowl LII. His podcast, Unblocked, returns September 9. PHLY also added two new Eagles contributors: Brandon Lee Gowton, founder of Bleeding Green Nation, and Miles Johnson, known for Real Talk with MJ. Both join returning voices Bo Wulf, EJ Smith, and Fran Duffy across pre- and postgame programming. 10 players to watch in the Eagles’ final preseason game vs. the Bengals – PhillyVoice iDL Uar Bernard and EDGE Joshua Weru: In the Patriots game, Weru dusted a Pats OT with a highly athletic Eurostep move, and Bernard made a couple of nice run stops. I have both Eagles “exchange dudes” on the initial 53-man roster after they proved throughout camp and in the preseason games that they have enticing traits that are worth developing over time. They’ll get one last chance to play in an NFL game this season before they’re buried on the depth chart during the regular season. How every 2026 NFL draft pick has looked in the preseason – ESPN Round 2 (No. 54): Eli Stowers, TE. It has been a slow start for Stowers. He has worked primarily with the second and third teams and hasn’t had many eye-catching moments in camp. Stowers needs to develop as a blocker, and while he has the mentality to do so by all accounts, it’s going to take time. He suffered a hamstring injury in the second preseason game against the Patriots. Round 3 (No. 68): Markel Bell, OT. Bell has been the best Eagles rookie this summer, looking smooth in pass protection while creating lanes in the run game. He is in position to serve as the swing tackle and might be Lane Johnson’s eventual replacement at right tackle. Eagles-Bengals week: 6 burning questions, from grading Jalen Hurts to training camp MVP – The Athletic How would you grade Jalen Hurts’ training camp? Berman: By letter grade, I’ll give him a B/B-. He practiced three weeks without DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon, and any quarterback would look better with Smith. Hurts adjusted to the offense and embraced changes to footwork, cadence, operating under center, and throwing across the middle. Hurts calls it “sponge mode” this time of year. There’s something to be said about his willingness to embrace change at this point in his career. He made several high-level passes that Super Bowl MVPs and franchise quarterbacks make. But there were more inconsistencies than in previous summers, with inefficient practice. There were also far more interceptions. We’ll see what translates to games. I’ve also been impressed by his mobility and am curious how that factors into the offense this season. He’s had better camps in the past with A.J. Brown and Smith on the field. But Brown’s not here this season, so that point is moot. The key is keeping Smith (and Lemon) healthy. I’d be concerned about the passing game without him. As Eagles adopt more aggressive offense, Jalen Hurts ‘not afraid of making mistakes’ – Yahoo! Sports The Eagles believe their wide receiver room features versatility in the wake of trading A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots on June 1 for a 2028 first-round draft pick and 2027 fifth. Former Green Bay Packers receiver Dontayvion Wicks, 2026 first-round selection Makai Lemon and journeyman 2019 first-rounder Hollywood Brown join a room led by DeVonta Smith, who’s coming off his third 1,000-yard season in the last four years. “You have a No. 1 receiver in DeVonta Smith, who, we’ve always believed has been a No. 1 receiver,” Sirianni said. “You have a ‘Tay Wicks who I think has great qualities of a wide receiver: I always think that my ideal receiver in the NFL, before I look at speed and before I look at anything else, [has] play strength and body quickness [to get] in and out of the breaks. And this guy has elite of both.” Brown and Elijah Moore will be tabbed to add further speed while Darius Cooper will step up for “dirty work,” Sirianni said. title: Vote now for the 2026 Isaac Redman Award
summary: The time has finally come for Behind the Steel Curtain’s most prestigious tradition: The Isaac Redman Award. Now over a decade old (and with its own section on Wikipedia), the award, in the words of former BTSC editor Neal Coolong, is to be given to “the unheralded Steelers player who came from the furthest reaches […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 4: Running back Isaac Redman #33 of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs for a one yard touchdown against the New York Giants in the fourth quarter during an NFL game at MetLife Stadium on November 4, 2012 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The Steelers defeated the Giants 24-20. (Photo by Rich Schultz /Getty Images) | Getty Images The time has finally come for Behind the Steel Curtain’s most prestigious tradition: The Isaac Redman Award. Now over a decade old (and with its own section on Wikipedia ), the award, in the words of former BTSC editor Neal Coolong, is to be given to “the unheralded Steelers player who came from the furthest reaches of obscurity to reach general heightened fame and appeal among Steelers fans.” As originally stated in that 2014 article, the basic rules are as follows: Eligibility Player must not be a draft pick higher than the sixth round Player can only have participated in two other training camps prior to this one Player demonstrated frequent references in comments regarding the likelihood of significant playing time in the coming year Weight of general fan sentiment leans towards the player being a “diamond in the rough” Player does not have to make the team in the year of his nomination to qualify (this isn’t meant to be included in 53-man roster discussion) Staff nominations Ryan Parish: This year, it was between two rookies for me: Gabe Rubio and Robert Spears-Jennings. Both impressed, but I’m going to give the nod to Rubio. In three games, the young nose tackle racked up six solo tackles and assisted on six others. He recorded five “Stops” which are plays PFF chart as tackles that produce a negative outcome for the offense. Rubio even managed two pressures the final preseason game against the Bills. There’s an argument that outside of Germie Bernard, he was the rookie with the most impressive preseason performance, which makes him the clear Redman winner on my ballot. Mike Nicastro: I’ll go off the grid a bit and give my nomination to Lew Nichols, who is a similar player to Isaac Redman in stature — he even won the award last year. Nichols just keeps on trucking. He led the team in rushing with 87 yards on 20 attempts – good for a 4.35 average. He also scored a touchdown and probably should have had another if he kept his balance on a great run in their first contest against the Packers. He isn’t going to necessarily be the belle of any ball, but he deserves some recognition, and possibly a roster spot, for his consistency and relentless approach. Jarrett Bailey : I’ll give mine to Robert Spears-Jennings. With the depth at safety (or lack thereof) being a big question, the seventh-round pick had a very strong summer in camp and in preseason play. He should get a spot on the 53-man roster. Joey Bray: It would be a shame if the Pittsburgh kid Eli Heidenreich didn’t get a nomination for the Redman Award. Steelers fans rejoiced when the Mt. Lebanon high school alumni was selected 240th overall back in April. Heidenreich’s middle name is versatility, playing wide receiver and running back in college. His awareness and ability in the open field makes him a serious big play threat and giving Mike McCarthy no shortage of ways to use him. The Steelers primarily used Heidenreich as a running back throughout the summer. After missing a few weeks in camp with a leg injury, his spot on the 53-man roster doesn’t seem to be a lock. Heidenreich played well in the Steelers preseason finale, scoring a touchdown and getting some run as a return man on special teams. “The Swiss Navy Knife” deserves a spot on the 53-man roster, and potentially a Redman Award victory. Ryland Bickley: While my vote will almost certainly go to one of Rubio or Spears-Jennings (please convince me which one), I’d be remiss if I didn’t get Will Howard onto this ballot as a former sixth-rounder who dominated preseason talking points even when his on-field performance didn’t always live up to the hype. Sure, Howard didn’t come from the depths of obscurity as a former National Championship-winning Ohio State quarterback, but he’s built up a fanbase worthy of Redman Award consideration, leading to discussion of the Steelers keeping a whopping four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster just to keep Howard from potentially being poached by another team. The point of this award is to recognize August storylines with a bit too much hype, and while Howard still has plenty of time to develop, I’m not sure if another player better encapsulates that sense of preseason overreaction than him. Other notable eligibles DB Devan Boykin DL Kevin Jobity Jr. TE Lake McRee WR Max Hurleman DB Doneiko Slaughter WR Brandon Smith OLB Julius Welschof LB Carson Bruener Vote! But enough of what the staff wants to say — this is your decision! Vote below in the poll, and if you want to write in an eligible candidate, recs on a comment stating a player’s candidacy will count as votes. The ballot will stay open through Saturday, with the winner announced before the cutdown deadline on Sunday. May the best Isaac Redman Award candidate win, joining a storied fraternity that includes the likes of Mike Hilton, Roosevelt Nix, and Tyler Matakevich. And make sure to fill the comment section with civil discourse election propaganda below.
author: Ryan Parish

title: The Morning After: Keeping four QBs is bad roster building
summary: The end of preseason has always been the unofficial beginning of fall in my eyes. As I stare out my window, I can see a hint of color becoming more prevalent in the trees, the sun is setting earlier with each passing day, and the pumpkin coffee I have sitting next to me tastes like […]
full_text: Aug 27, 2026; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Will Howard (18) looks to pass the ball against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the third quarter at New Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The end of preseason has always been the unofficial beginning of fall in my eyes. As I stare out my window, I can see a hint of color becoming more prevalent in the trees, the sun is setting earlier with each passing day, and the pumpkin coffee I have sitting next to me tastes like I’ll be turning on Halloween 6 later on in the day. The preseason is now complete for the Pittsburgh Steelers, and they will now have until Sunday night at 6:00 EST to trim their roster down to 53 players. And while the journey will end for many, it appears one player on the bubble has a spot secured. Plus, a pair of rookie receivers show exactly why they were drafted, and several defenders will make it very difficult to let them go. It’s the morning after game day. Let’s dive in. The Steelers should not keep four quarterbacks After the Steelers’ 28-27 loss to the Bills to close out the preseason, head coach Mike McCarthy was asked if all four quarterbacks did enough to secure a roster spot. “Very accurate evaluation on your part,” McCarthy said via Brooke Pryor. “We’ve got two vets to win with, and two guys we’re excited about their future.” Of course, nothing is official at the time of writing, but it certainly appears as if the Steelers will keep all four quarterbacks on their roster, which makes next to no sense. It would be one thing if Will Howard blew them away in exhibition play – he didn’t. He finished the preseason 26-of-40 with two touchdowns to three interceptions. For what it’s worth, both touchdowns he threw were a screen pass that Germie Bernard took 13 yards after making the first tackler miss, and practically a handoff to Lake McRee who dove over several players to get into the end zone. That’s not to see there weren’t good throws. The pass to Robert Tonyan on the goal line in Week 1 against the Packers was his best throw of the preseason, and he made a 16-yard completion to Ben Skowronek over the middle in Week 2. However, if he really popped, the Steelers wouldn’t feel the need to keep Mason Rudolph. Howard was comfortably the fourth-best quarterback for the Steelers throughout the summer. The logical decision would be to cut him and then sign him to the practice squad when no one claims him. Everyone in the Will Howard camp is so certain he would get claimed by another team, but that’s highly unlikely to happen. About 25-35 players total get claimed during roster cutdown. Last year, there were 29 players claimed. The year before that – 27, per Saad Yousuf of The Athletic . The high since 2015 is 44 players . The low is 17, which came back in 2020. Howard didn’t do anything in exhibition play to warrant a team putting in a claim for him. He would quickly have a home back on the Steelers’ practice squad should that be the route they would go. Instead, they will likely keep Howard, assuming he doesn’t go on IR with an injury he suffered against the Bills. Even if he does go on IR, though, eventually they’d have to take him off, which would lead to the team eventually carrying four quarterbacks. Who’s the player that will lose their helmet because of it? Robert Spears-Jennings? Doneiko Slaughter? Both of whom have had tremendous summers. If Howard gets a spot over someone who can contribute elsewhere, it’s roster building malpractice. Germie Bernard is WR3 I’ve seen enough from Bernard – he absolutely should be the starting slot receiver. The Alabama product has shown more this preseason than Roman Wilson has going on three seasons. It’s great that Wilson looked good in camp. It means nothing, though, when he does nothing come game time. Bernard showcased exactly why the Steelers traded up to get him, making Max Hairston miss on a screen pass and taking it the rest of the way to the end zone. He finished his preseason with five catches for 64 yards and a touchdown. And as impressive as his first (unofficial) touchdown was, it may not have been his best play of the preseason. In Week 1 against the Packers, he caught a ball on the right sideline made several defenders miss, and picked up 25 yards. The best thing the Steelers could do at receiver right now is give Bernard the No. 3 spot on the depth chart, see if they can get a late-round pick swap in exchange for Roman Wilson, and sign a veteran to be the No. 4 wide receiver Brandin Cooks would be the name I’d prefer. He’s still a quality deep threat, and he had a nice pair of seasons under McCarthy from 2023-24, catching 80 passes and 11 touchdowns in that two-year span. Kaden Wetjen puts exclamation point on preseason The rookie out of Iowa began the preseason with a 74-yard catch and a touchdown, and he ended it by showing exactly why the Steelers took him in the fourth round. The two-time Jet Award winner struggled to get anything going in the return game in the first half. In the third quarter, though, he sprung away from the Bills’ punt coverage and returned a kick 45 yards for a touchdown. Should he be able to house at least one kick during the regular season, many will forget about the Steelers reaching in the fourth for a return specialist. While he rode the highs and lows of his first NFL training camp, the highs are very high for one of the best return men in college football history. Several defenders make their case for roster spots There will be at least one defender worthy of a roster spot who doesn’t get one – which, again, makes the likelihood of Will Howard having a spot even more irrational. Devan Boykin had a strong preseason and led the team with nine tackles on Thursday. D’Shawn Jamison has been a practice squad mainstay for Pittsburgh over the last two years and appeared in three games in 2025. He’ll likely be placed on the practice squad again despite a nice preseason. Slaughter and Spears-Jennings are another pair of guys who are on that roster bubble, and one or both could be placed on the practice squad. Having a lot of quality players is a good problem to have, and Pittsburgh may have one of the deeper set of reserves in the NFL once Week 1 rolls around. Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! title: 5 takeaways from the Steelers’ 28-27 loss to the Buffalo Bills
summary: The Steelers ended their preseason with a one-point loss to the Buffalo Bills. The final score doesn’t matter, but the play of those involved certainly impacted the rapidly-approaching NFL cutdown deadline. As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had. 1. Rookie playmakers make plays While it’s only the preseason, I’ve been impressed with […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 27: Eli Heidenreich #29 of the Pittsburgh Steelers celebrates his touchdown with Drew Allar #16 of the Pittsburgh Steelers during the second half against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Steelers ended their preseason with a one-point loss to the Buffalo Bills. The final score doesn’t matter, but the play of those involved certainly impacted the rapidly-approaching NFL cutdown deadline. As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had. 1. Rookie playmakers make plays While it’s only the preseason, I’ve been impressed with how second-round wide receiver Germie Bernard’s yards after catch ability has transferred from college to the pros. Bernard recorded the best play of his NFL career thus far against the Bills, turning a short throw in the flats into the first touchdown of the game. Rookie WR Germie Bernard breaks the tackle on the way to the touchdown! PITvsBUF on @NFLNetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1NbNFYPcri — NFL (@NFL) August 27, 2026 The play showed off some wiggle in the open field, but also the play strength to shrug off a tackle attempt. Bernard’s preseason hasn’t been spectacular, per se, but he seems to be on the right track towards becoming a contributor on offense. And if the Steelers’ passing game continues to rely on quick concepts with Aaron Rodgers in 2026, having another receiver that can turn a short throw into a big gain will be a great fit. Also impressing was seventh-round running back Eli Heidenreich, who made a last-minute push for the Steelers’ RB3 spot ahead of cutdown day. His nine carries for 35 yards and a touchdown don’t necessarily leap off the page, but I thought he looked incredibly light on his feet and a bit more decisive as a runner this week — it also helped he had better running lanes this time around than in games past. I still think Heidenreich looks a little slight for an NFL running back, but he did a good job keeping his momentum through contact on Thursday. He also showed off some special teams value, getting involved in at least one tackle and recording a team-best 26-yard kickoff return. Odds are still that he takes a redshirt year on the practice squad, but I felt that the rookie had his best showing in the preseason finale. And I’m still waiting for the Steelers to give him a chance to show what he can do as a pass-catcher. Saving the best for last, it was fourth-round receiver and return specialist Kaden Wetjen who provided the team’s moment of the game with a 45-yard punt return touchdown in the fourth quarter right as it felt like all of Steelers Twitter had finally turned on him. The rookie Kaden Wetjen maneuvers his way all the way to the end zone! PITvsBUF on @NFLNetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gjtNooO9D6 — NFL (@NFL) August 28, 2026 Wetjen had a rough outing last week against the Jets, and had started off the Buffalo game with returns that varied from “fine” to “why are you running sideways.” Then, in his last quarter before cutdown day, he runs east-west, retraces his steps, and delivers the most electric touchdown of the game. I actually laughed at the timing. Well played, rookie. I’m excited to see what Wetjen does next. 2. The QB battle ends not with a bang, but a whimper OK, that’s a little dramatic, but for all the hype about seeing Will Howard and Drew Allar playing in Steelers uniforms for the first time this summer — and some undeniably solid plays this month — Week 3 of the preseason delivered some lukewarm performances at best. Howard’s two touchdowns certainly aren’t a bad thing, but the stat sheet didn’t tell the full story, with the pass-catcher doing the bulk of the work on each score after fairly easy, short completions. Howard also upped his total to three interceptions this preseason, adding another turnover on what looked like a miscommunication between him and rookie tight end Lake McRee. Update: the interception is both on Steelers QB Will Howard and TE Lake McRee. Howard is an enigma, but what we know is that he's definitely not a QB1. pic.twitter.com/NVsU1RaanC — Steelers Black and Gold Nation – Preseason (@B_GNation1) August 27, 2026 More frustrating was how Howard looked under pressure, taking some rough sacks and just not looking the most composed or mobile. Allar came in for the second half and, as always, looked like the more natural athlete, but completed just half of his pass attempts for no touchdowns and a mere 88 yards (still 19 more than Howard). Allar nearly threw an interception himself, throwing the ball right to a cornerback in what also looked like a quarterback/receiver miscommunication. Without knowing exactly what either player was supposed to do there, it’s hard to judge, but it didn’t look like a great decision throwing the ball on a slant when a defender had such heavy inside leverage. Allar missed on some deeper, “touch” throws later in the game, as well. All that to say, neither young passer did much to further their agenda Thursday night, and at this point it will be surprising to see anyone other than Mason Rudolph listed at QB2 entering the regular season. Still, I would’ve liked to see Allar take a few snaps with a more competent group of receivers at some point this preseason — the rookie passer certainly had his warts, but his pass-catchers really haven’t done much to help him out over the past few weeks. But for now, Allar remains firmly in the raw-but-intriguing QB3 position, while Howard will likely start his September as a stash on the practice squad or maybe injured reserve . 3. Rookie O-linemen are promising, but not ready yet After a disappointing performance from the Steelers’ offensive line last week, I pointed out that both of the team’s big investments in that group this year — first-round tackle Max Iheanachor and third-round guard Gennings Dunker — didn’t even play. However, both saw the field against Buffalo, and while neither stole the show, both looked like players who could certainly contribute down the road. Of course, it wasn’t all good. Dunker was beat badly for an interior pressure at one point: This is killing me 😭 pic.twitter.com/SApEiwSUrL — (Not) Art Rooney II (@OldManRooney) August 27, 2026 And Iheanachor also had a notably bad pass protection rep, along with a holding penalty that probably shouldn’t have been called and a possible false start that he might’ve gotten away with. A replay of the Max Iheanachor sack pic.twitter.com/YCvb2bDqcy — LandonTengwall (@LandonTengwall) August 28, 2026 There was a lot of good too, though. While Iheanachor probably isn’t the team’s top right tackle immediately, he already looks more controlled than Broderick Jones as a mover, and more solid as an anchor than Dylan Cook. A play that summed up both players’ strengths well was actually Eli Heidenreich‘s third-quarter touchdown, where the rookies paved the way for their fellow 2026 draft class member.
