title: NFL waiver wire rules and the Steelers’ position in the waiver order
summary: With the NFL preseason nearing its conclusion, teams will have to begin the process of cutting players to be compliant with the 53-man limit for the regular season. The Steelers themselves just played their final preseason game and will need to make some tough decisions by the cutdown deadline this Sunday, August 30, by 6 […]
full_text: Nov 17, 2024; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers general manager Omar Khan talks on the phone before the game against the Baltimore Ravens at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con With the NFL preseason nearing its conclusion, teams will have to begin the process of cutting players to be compliant with the 53-man limit for the regular season. The Steelers themselves just played their final preseason game and will need to make some tough decisions by the cutdown deadline this Sunday, August 30, by 6 PM EST. As Pittsburgh gets one step closer to the regular season, they enter the year at plus-money odds to make the postseason at +154, per FanDuel Sportsbook . The flurry of transactions won’t stop after initial cuts, though. Every year, after teams announce who they’ve released, there is a waiver process that allows teams to claim certain players released by other organizations. Which players are eligible for these claims? When must claims be made? And how does the NFL decide the waiver order? We’ve got the answers for you. When is the waiver deadline? Once the 53-man roster deadline arrives, teams will have until 1 PM EST the next day — August 31 this year — to file their claims. The NFL will review those claims and then announce which claims were successful shortly after the deadline. Once those have been announced, teams will officially be able to start filling their practice squads. Which players can go on waivers? The NFL ecosystem contains a great many players. During the preseason, teams are allowed up to 90 players on their rosters at a time, which works out to 2,880 players. But once cutdowns occur, just 1,696 remain, meaning 1,184 are suddenly up for grabs for teams to add if they wish. Some of those players will head to the waiver wire, but others won’t. To determine which players are which, the NFL sorts the players into two categories: players who are vested and players who are not. A vested player is one who has been credited with four or more seasons of NFL experience. To be credited for an NFL season , a player must have been on the active, inactive, IR, or PUP roster for three or more regular-season or postseason games. A player can also be credited for a season if they receive an injury settlement or grievance for the equivalent of three or more regular-season games. Note that a credited season is different from accrued seasons , which determine what type of free agent a player is. Vested players do not go onto waivers and are free to sign with any team at any time, between the day after the Super Bowl and the NFL trade deadline. They are subject to waivers in the period after the deadline through the Super Bowl. Non-vested players, or players with three or fewer credited seasons, are subject to waivers. If these players go unclaimed, they are free to negotiate with teams as free agents. How does the NFL determine waiver wire priority? Through the first three weeks of the NFL season, the waiver reorder follows the order of that season’s draft. Trades in the draft are ignored for this process, so, for example, the Bengals — who traded out of the 10th spot — would still be 10th in waiver priority. That means the Steelers will be 21st in waiver priority. It’s also important to note that the NFL doesn’t have a rolling waiver system like readers who play fantasy football might be familiar with. In fantasy football, a successful claim typically moves a team down in waiver priority so they can’t hog all the waiver claims. However, in the NFL, a team in the top priority gets as many of their claims as they want. If that team filed 53 claims, they’d get all 53 if they wanted them. Obviously, no organization is going to go to that extreme, which is why teams are allowed to prioritize and add specifications to these claims. Using our example, a team could file 53 claims, number those claims in priority 1-53, and say something along the lines of “we only want two receivers and a cornerback,” which would cancel all their other claims once their specifications have been met. What’s the current waiver order? title: Steelers stock report after 28-27 preseason loss to Buffalo Bills
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers fell to the Buffalo Bills 28-27 in their 2026 preseason finale. After jumping out to a 14-3 lead early in the first quarter, Bills quarterback Shane Buechele led a game-winning touchdown drive to give Buffalo the win. More importantly, we got to see pivotal performances from some players who had to make […]
full_text: Aug 27, 2026; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver Germie Bernard (17) avoids a tackle Buffalo Bills defensive back Maxwell Hairston (31) during the first quarter at New Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers fell to the Buffalo Bills 28-27 in their 2026 preseason finale. After jumping out to a 14-3 lead early in the first quarter, Bills quarterback Shane Buechele led a game-winning touchdown drive to give Buffalo the win. More importantly, we got to see pivotal performances from some players who had to make their final impressions before teams cut down to a 53-man roster this Sunday. Let’s take a look at who improved their stock, and who hurt theirs during the Steelers preseason finale. Stock up: WR Germie Bernard After being held without a catch on his lone target last week, Bernard made the most of his one catch by scoring a first-quarter touchdown in the Steelers preseason finale. Bernard took a screen pass and made a move on former first-round pick Maxwell Hairston on his way to the end zone. Bernard has shown great ability after the catch throughout the preseason and will likely have a role with the starters at some point during his rookie season. KR Kaden Wetjen I’ll be completely honest here, when I was drafting this piece up during the second half I had penciled in Kaden Wetjen under the “stock down category.” Not five minutes after I did so, Wetjen made the play of the preseason with a 45-yard punt return touchdown. The rookie fourth-round pick went backwards on two of his punt returns in the first half and had struggled throughout the preseason until that moment. That play all but secures Wetjen a roster spot as the Steelers’ primary return man. OT Max Iheanachor The Steelers’ 2026 first-round pick made his long-awaited NFL debut after missing a few weeks with a shoulder/neck injury. Iheanachor was almost immediately blown by and gave up a sack on his first series on the field. Later, the rookie was flagged on a very questionable call for a hold. Max Iheanachor holding call which I think is a garbage call. Destroy all refs who think snatch and trap is a holding call https://t.co/znYvB0AJUK pic.twitter.com/lykn3RW4b1 — LandonTengwall (@LandonTengwall) August 28, 2026 In the second half, Iheanachor made a phenomenal downfield block to clear the way for rookie running back Eli Heidenreich to stroll into the end zone. For limited reps in a debut, Iheanachor showed serious promise, and given the struggles by the Steelers’ starting line this preseason, he could become a starter sooner rather than later. Stock down: QB Will Howard Will Howard threw his third interception of the preseason in the first half on what was clearly a miscommunication between Howard and his tight end Lake McRee. Whether Howard or McRee is more at fault is unclear, but Howard’s sloppy handling of the ball will almost certainly cost him the backup job. Pocket presence also seems to be a major area of concern for Howard. Too many times in this game, Howard either did not step up in the pocket and get sacked, or tried to extend the play for too long and got sacked. The second-year quarterback did throw two touchdowns early in the contest after being put in favorable positions due to a muffed punt and a shanked punt by Buffalo. Howard’s future with the Steelers will be dependent on whether or not the team decides to keep four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster. RB Kaleb Johnson After pacing the team in carries last week touched the ball just five times for 11 yards in this contest. After solid performances by Lew Nichols and Eli Heidenreich, any glimmer of hope for Johnson to make the roster may have dissipated. The 2025 third-round pick will be in danger of being cut when rosters are finalized by Sunday at 6 p.m. OT Dylan Cook Read into this how you will, but Dylan Cook started this game at left tackle despite being slated to start at right tackle this season. It was Broderick Jones starting at right tackle. Cook did end up playing some at right tackle, and even played into the second half. It seems like the Steelers are at least considering the idea of not starting Cook to begin the season. Given Cook’s struggles throughout preseason and Iheanachor’s solid debut, it seems to only be a matter of time before Cook loses his starting spot. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Kaden Wetjen locks up roster spot as Steelers close preseason with loss to Bills
summary: The best thing about the Pittsburgh Steelers’ preseason finale against the Buffalo Bills is that it’s now over. I’m only kidding. Sort of. The Steelers closed their preseason with a 28-27 loss to the Buffalo Bills. With this being the final exhibition contest, it also marked the final chance for several players to show they […]
full_text: Aug 27, 2026; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver Kaden Wetjen (10) carries the ball for a touchdown against the Buffalo Bills during the fourth quarter at New Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The best thing about the Pittsburgh Steelers’ preseason finale against the Buffalo Bills is that it’s now over. I’m only kidding. Sort of. The Steelers closed their preseason with a 28-27 loss to the Buffalo Bills. With this being the final exhibition contest, it also marked the final chance for several players to show they are worthy of a roster spot. Of course, a lot of the attention would be on the quarterback position, as Will Howard and Drew Allar were once again the only two quarterbacks to take the field. Despite Howard throwing a pair of interceptions in Week 2 against the New York Jets, he was the starter to close out the preseason, which started with a sack on the first play of scrimmage for the offense. The Steelers punted after a three-and-out, but were bailed out by a muffed punt from Bills running back Ray Davis. On the ensuing play, Germie Bernard took a screen pass 13 yards for a touchdown, making cornerback Max Hairston miss in the open field on his way to the end zone. The Steelers got another break on special teams, as Bills punter Mitch Witchnowski shanked a punt, setting the Steelers up inside the 30 yard-line. Five plays later, Lake McRee took a short pass and dove over Bills defenders into the end zone for a five yard score. And while Howard had a pair of touchdowns to his name in the box score, his play was subpar, to say the least. While facing pressure, he went 2-of-4 for a net of -7 yards and three sacks. He also threw his third interception of the preseason on a ball that looked as if it was intended for Bills safety Damar Hamlin. And while it looked as if there was a miscommunication between quarterback and receiver, three interceptions in exhibition play is incredibly difficult to defend. Howard ended his day going 9-of-15 for 69 yards and the aforementioned two touchdowns and interception. Drew Allar led a touchdown-scoring drive to open the second half. An 11-play, 68-yard drive saw Allar go 3-of-4 for 34 yards, including a 25 yard completion to Max Hurleman, and was capped off with a nine-yard touchdown run by Eli Heidenreich. The touchdown run featured a great lead block by rookie right tackle Max Iheanachor, who led the way for Heidenreich and cleared a path for him at the goal line. The play of the night, though, came once again from the Steelers’ special teams unit. After a slow night, Kaden Wetjen took a punt 45 yards for a touchdown to put the Steelers up 27-17, showing exactly why the Steelers felt comfortable spending a fourth-round pick on him. The Bills would come back and score 11 unanswered points to take a 28-27 lead. Pittsburgh had a chance to drive downfield to kick a potential game-winning field goal, but turned the ball over on downs after three incompletions, leading to the 28-27 loss. Allar finished the night 9-of-18 for 88 yards. While the main focus was on the offense and the quarterback play, multiple defenders did all they could to put on good final impressions. Devan Boykin led the team with nine tackles, and D’Shawn Jamison had a pair of tackles for loss and broke up a pass. Julius Welschof also netted a pair of tackles for loss and a sack, while Anthony Goodflow and Kevin Jobity each registered a sack a piece. Robert Spears-Jennings continues to impress, and it will be very hard to see him not get a spot on the 53-man roster. Elandon Roberts picked up where he left off against the Jets and looks keen to get on the field in Week 1. Offensively, Hurleman finished the evening with three catches for 50 yards, and Lew Nichols closed out an impressive summer by leading all Steelers rushers with 40 yards on seven carries. With the preseason now over, the Steelers will begin making their final roster cuts down to 53 before getting ready to officially open their season against the Atlanta Falcons. title: 12 Seahawks bubble players to watch vs. Chiefs
summary: It’s the last week of preseason, which means roster cuts are on the horizon for the Seattle Seahawks and the rest of the NFL. With Seattle retaining so many of its players from last season, the roster bubble is probably a bit smaller than most other teams, but nevertheless still compelling. Let’s get to some […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 23: Michael Dansby #37 and Maxen Hook #43 of the Seattle Seahawks break up a pass intended for Bryce Oliver #80 of the Tennessee Titans during the second half of Week 2 of the preseason game at Nissan Stadium on August 23, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s the last week of preseason, which means roster cuts are on the horizon for the Seattle Seahawks and the rest of the NFL. With Seattle retaining so many of its players from last season, the roster bubble is probably a bit smaller than most other teams, but nevertheless still compelling. Let’s get to some roster bubble talk before the Seahawks take on the Kansas City Chiefs at 5 pm PT at Arrowhead Stadium. And no, Jalen Milroe is not on this list. You were going to be watching Milroe regardless of whether he was on the bubble or not, so this is about filling out positions for which the depth is a bit questionable. Running Back: Jacardia Wright and Velus Jones Jr It’s possible that neither player makes the cut, if only because Seattle likely has its three running backs (Jadarian Price, George Holani, and Emanuel Wilson) for the regular season. When Zach Charbonnet comes back, they’ll have four. Wright and Jones can both be practice squad stashes and game day elevations for a few weeks, if needed. Wright returned from injury last week and rocketed his way into the end zone on a 69-yard touchdown run. Jones has had a good camp in his first proper offseason as a running back, plus he has experience (albeit not great ones in the NFL) as a wide receiver. The edge probably goes to Wright IF Seattle keeps a fourth running back, I suspect. Wide Receiver: Montorie Foster Jr, Cody White, Emmanuel Henderson, Ricky White III I contemplated leaving Foster off completely because I think he has a spot secured, but let me not get ahead of my skis and risk him being the new Kasen Williams or Easop Winston. Foster should have an inside track, but Cody White has the most experience of this group, Emmanuel Henderson has done pretty much nothing at receiver but could be a very good special teams players, and Ricky White III is another special teams standout. With Jake Bobo’s season over , will the Seahawks roster five receivers or six? This could be two spots for the aforementioned four or everyone competing for the fifth and final spot. Foster has been the best actual wide receiver among this quartet, with Henderson maybe the most versatile on special teams. Cornerback: Andre Fuller, Michael Dansby, and Trevon Diggs I’ve left off Noah Igbinoghene if only because he’s a vested veteran and doesn’t have to go through waivers. There’s a chance that, in order to roster one of Fuller or Dansby, the Seahawks get creative and “cut” Igbinoghene and sign him after the practice squads have formed. Even still, from what I’ve seen of Noah I believe he has value on this roster. Fuller has been exclusively a slot corner in preseason, which is interesting to see. Dansby had the more eye-popping camp and his speed and quickness to the ball-carrier is something that has stood out at times. They’ve had their respective ups and downs with their camp and preseason reps, but I think the Seahawks would like to have at least one of these guys on the roster. Then there’s Trevon Diggs. He says he’s had a healthy offseason for the first time, but now it’s time to see him in live game reps. The former Dallas Cowboys All-Pro corner has had a tough go of it with injuries and lackluster performances over the previous three years, so this is his first chance to show there’s still something left in the tank. There’s obvious uncertainty as far as the cornerback depth below Josh Jobe and Devon Witherspoon. Do the Seahawks address this with a higher volume of CBs than normal? Nehemiah Pritchett should be fine, as should Igbinoghene even if they do funny roster tricks with him, but it’s still up for grabs as far as remaining spots. There’s also, of course, the looming Terrion Arnold signing, although he’s set to be on the commissioner’s exempt list the minute the ink is dry. Safety: A.J. Finley, D’Anthony Bell, and Maxen Hook I’m leaving Rodney Thomas II off if only because I don’t know if he’s playing tonight. He had recent hand surgery and even then was spending a fair amount of time with the third-team in his lone preseason outing versus the Dallas Cowboys. There are question marks about Nick Emmanwori’s Week 1 readiness and, of course, who will step up now that Bud Clark’s Week 1 readiness is for the 2027 season. Finley could be a great turnaround story after tearing his ACL last training camp, and he’s generally been the starting deep safety over the last two preseason outings. Bell is really more an approximation of Emmanwori’s presence down in the box, and he’s someone Seattle could keep even temporarily as Emmanwori insurance. Hook has drawn some praise from Coach Mike Mcadonald and had a good game (particularly his tackling) versus the Tennessee Titans. If Ty Okada, Julian Love, and Nick Emmanwori are roster locks, we might see the Seahawks keep a maximum of two additional safeties out of the aforementioned three (well, maybe four if we include Thomas). title: Seahawks 2026 draft class facing uphill battle after Julian Neal, Bud Clark injuries
summary: The Seattle Seahawks entered the 2026 season with plenty of young players looking for an opportunity, but the path from draft pick to NFL contributor is rarely straightforward. For Seattle’s rookie class, that process has already become more complicated. So far, Jadarian Price appears to be the only realistic option from the class to contribute […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks entered the 2026 season with plenty of young players looking for an opportunity, but the path from draft pick to NFL contributor is rarely straightforward. For Seattle’s rookie class, that process has already become more complicated. So far, Jadarian Price appears to be the only realistic option from the class to contribute immediately as a rookie. Bud Clark is out for the season after suffering a broken ankle on Seattle’s first defensive snap against the Tennessee Titans. Julian Neal is also dealing with an injury that has yet to be fully explained by the team. Those injuries matter, but they are only part of the story. The bigger question surrounding Seattle’s 2026 draft class may be much simpler: how many of these rookies will actually earn a place on the 53-man roster? Clark was one of the rookies with the clearest opportunity to carve out a role in Mike Macdonald’s defense. The second-round pick out of TCU brought the versatility and coverage ability Seattle was looking for in its secondary, and his ability to contribute in different packages made him an appealing fit for the defense. Instead, his rookie season is already over. Neal presents a different situation. The third-round cornerback out of Arkansas had a legitimate opportunity to compete for playing time at a position where Seattle has several questions behind its top options. His injury now removes another young player from that competition, at least temporarily. That could have a significant effect on the roster battle at cornerback. With Neal unavailable, veterans such as Trevon Diggs and Noah Igbinoghene become more important, while Seattle has fewer opportunities to evaluate its younger options. If Neal’s injury keeps him out for an extended period, the Seahawks may ultimately have to decide whether they have enough depth at the position or whether they need to look outside the building. But losing Clark and Neal doesn’t mean the draft class itself is in trouble. In fact, the more immediate concern is what happens with the rest of the rookies. Seattle has several other draft picks (notably Michael Dansby and Andre Fuller) competing for roster spots, and some of them face a much steeper climb than Clark or Neal did. By the end of August, the Seahawks have to determine which rookies have done enough to justify occupying one of 53 roster spots. That’s where preseason performance becomes particularly important. Beau Stephens is one of the more interesting examples. There was some discussion that Stephens could potentially emerge as a player capable of challenging Anthony Bradford for the starting job. I’m considerably less convinced that’s where the competition currently stands. Stephens has shown flashes, but he hasn’t demonstrated the kind of consistent jump that would make me believe he’s ready to unseat an established player. And, to be fair, some of what we’ve seen is perfectly normal for a rookie. There have been good reps followed by mistakes. Plays where his technique and athleticism stand out, followed by snaps where he looks like exactly what he is: a young player still adjusting to the speed and physicality of the NFL. That isn’t necessarily a bad sign. Preseason is supposed to expose those inconsistencies, particularly for rookies. The important question is whether Stephens can turn those flashes into something more consistent as the evaluation period progresses. For now, however, I wouldn’t frame him as the player who is going to take Bradford’s job, and that distinction matters when evaluating this draft class. The Seahawks don’t need every rookie to become a starter. They need enough of them to become useful NFL players. Some will have obvious paths to playing time. Others may need to earn their roster spots through special teams, rotational snaps or simply demonstrating enough developmental potential for the coaching staff to keep them around. That could be the first real test of Seattle’s 2026 class. Clark is already lost for the season. Neal’s availability is uncertain. Meanwhile, several of the other rookies still have to prove that they belong on the roster in the first place. That’s a very different challenge from simply finding immediate production. And it is why the final week of preseason will tell us much more about this draft class than the draft grades ever could. If several of Seattle’s remaining rookies emerge as legitimate contributors, Clark’s injury and Neal’s absence can eventually become footnotes in what could still be a successful class. If, however, multiple picks fail to separate themselves from the veteran and undrafted competition, Seattle could finish the season with surprisingly little rookie production despite investing significant draft capital. That’s the real concern right now. The Seahawks don’t need this class to dominate in 2026. They need to identify which players can help them now, which players need more development and, perhaps most importantly, which players are worth keeping on the 53-man roster. Clark won’t get the opportunity to answer that question this year. Neal may have to wait before getting his chance. For everyone else, the battle is just beginning.

summary: Much like last year, the final preseason game will be a showcase opportunity for Seattle Seahawks quarterback Jalen Milroe. Mike Macdonald told reporters after Thursday’s practice that not only will starters sit out Friday’s tilt with the Kansas City Chiefs, but that Milroe, not Drew Lock, will get the start and play the whole way. […]
full_text: Seattle Seahawks quarterback Jalen Milroe (6) runs the ball against the Green Bay Packers during their final preseason game on Saturday, August 23, 2025, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. The Packers won the game, 20-7. Tork Mason/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Much like last year, the final preseason game will be a showcase opportunity for Seattle Seahawks quarterback Jalen Milroe. Mike Macdonald told reporters after Thursday’s practice that not only will starters sit out Friday’s tilt with the Kansas City Chiefs, but that Milroe, not Drew Lock, will get the start and play the whole way. Mike Macdonald said Seahawks starters who haven’t been playing in the preseason won’t play in the finale tomorrow at Kansas City. That includes RB Jadarian Price. QB3 Jalen Milroe will play the whole game. Also, he said WR Tory Horton’s injury isn’t a long-term thing. pic.twitter.com/J8b1ATWrAh — Brady Henderson (@BradyHenderson) August 27, 2026 “It’s great that he has the opportunity, just like the Green Bay game last year where you’re not subbing in, you’re not coming in at halftime,” Macdonald said. “You’re going through the whole process of starting a game and getting in rhythm and managing the situations. All those things that we want from our quarterback. It’s exciting to see him play, it’s a great opportunity for him.” If, for some reason, Milroe can’t continue, then Lock would be ready to step in. Milroe started the whole of the Green Bay Packers game as a rookie in 2025, completing 13 of 24 passes for 148 yards and a touchdown to Cody White. He also rushed for 31 yards but fumbled three times (losing all of them for turnovers). Whatever happens with the lineup, Milroe has an extended opportunity to showcase why the Seahawks took him in the third round back in 2025.

(Photo by Jeff Dean/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are on their way to Missouri for Friday’s preseason finale against the Kansas City Chiefs, and they’re taking a former Chiefs lineman with them. Per Thursday’s NFL transaction wire, the Seahawks claimed offensive tackle Kellen Diesch off waivers, one day after he was let go by the Chiefs. To make room on the 90-man roster, Seattle waived linebacker Chris Paul Jr. with an injury designation. Paul was one of the early bright spots against the Tennessee Titans for his run defense, although Paul has also been in-and-out of practice and preseason due to an ankle injury. If Paul is not claimed, he’ll revert to Seattle’s injured reserve. The 29-year-old Diesch is a well traveled journeyman who has been with seven NFL teams since 2022 and yet never played a regular season game. It was a great spring for Diesch, who was part of the UFL champion Louisville Kings roster, appearing in six games and starting in two. There’s not much reason to believe Diesch is anything but a preseason body to get a few snaps on Friday. Starters will not be playing, and it’s possible backup tackles like Josh Jones might get the night off, too. That leaves Diesch as a preseason depth option to go against a team he was with for six days.

title: Why Jalen Milroe’s development isn’t over, but it’s becoming a concern
summary: A few days ago, I wrote about my expectations for Jalen Milroe entering the preseason. At the time, I thought the most realistic goal for the Seahawks’ second-year quarterback was fairly simple: close the gap on Drew Lock and make the competition for the QB2 job a legitimate one. So far, that hasn’t happened. The […]
full_text: A few days ago, I wrote about my expectations for Jalen Milroe entering the preseason. At the time, I thought the most realistic goal for the Seahawks’ second-year quarterback was fairly simple: close the gap on Drew Lock and make the competition for the QB2 job a legitimate one. So far, that hasn’t happened. The reports coming out of training camp were encouraging in one regard. The Seahawks believe in Milroe and remain invested in his development. At the same time, head coach Mike Macdonald and Brian Fleury has made it clear that Milroe needs to show more as a quarterback if he wants to earn opportunities in more situations. Through two preseason games, that hasn’t really changed. Against the Dallas Cowboys, Seattle’s offense struggled, but Lock still looked more comfortable than Milroe. Against the Tennessee Titans, the gap was significantly larger. Milroe had a terrible game, finishing with two interceptions and another sack on fourth down. Outside of a few runs, he produced very little offensively. That doesn’t mean the Seahawks should give up on the project. Two preseason games are not enough to make that kind of decision, especially with a quarterback as young as Milroe. Everyone knew when Seattle drafted him that he would need time to refine his game. A bad preseason doesn’t suddenly change that. But there is a difference between understanding that a young quarterback needs development and seeing whether that development is actually happening. And so far, even compared with more conservative expectations for where Milroe should be at this point, he appears to be behind. The biggest issue isn’t necessarily his arm. It’s his willingness to use it. Seattle has actually put Milroe in some of the situations that I thought would make the most sense for him. Rollouts, play-action concepts and plays that reduce the number of reads he has to make while keeping his ability to run as part of the equation. But Milroe hasn’t consistently pulled the trigger. Whether it’s a lack of confidence or simply an attempt to play as conservatively as possible and avoid turnovers, the result is the same. He’s passing up opportunities to make plays, both as a passer and as a runner. That was particularly evident against the Titans. On the first interception, Milroe takes too long to deliver the ball, allowing the linebacker to read his eyes and get into the passing lane. That’s the kind of mistake that can happen with a young quarterback, but it’s also exactly the type of processing issue he needs to improve. Jalen Milroes escapa da pressão, mas demora para passar a bola e claramente, sem sinergia com o WR manda o passe atrás e gera uma interceptação para acabar com o jogo. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-27T01:30:15.426Z On the second interception, Milroe escapes the initial pressure (which came from Beau Stephens), keeps moving and once again finds some space to make a play. However, he hesitates for too long before delivering the ball. There is clearly no chemistry between him and wide receiver Emmanuel Henderson, and the pass ends up behind the receiver, who falls and allows the defender to make the interception that effectively ends the game. On 4th down sack- No one is open;- Holding on Nick VannettBut… – THROW IT MAN! — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-27T01:23:51.033Z The fourth-down sack was arguably even more frustrating. Milroe escapes the pocket trying to get away from the pressure, but instead of creating more space, he moves toward the linebacker who is sitting in a spy position. That makes the sack increasingly imminent. And once that happens, Milroe has to understand that holding onto the ball at all costs isn’t the right answer. Throw it. Maybe the defensive back intercepts it and takes it the other way. Maybe Nick Vannett, who appeared to be held on the play, makes a contested catch and converts the fourth down. There are plenty of possible outcomes, including a turnover. The one thing that’s certain is that getting sacked on fourth down ends the possession. That’s part of the development Milroe needs. He doesn’t have to play recklessly, but he also can’t be so afraid of making a mistake that he stops giving himself opportunities to make plays. That’s particularly concerning because running the football has been his best contribution so far, and he rushed just once in the Titans game. If the passing window isn’t there, Milroe has the athletic ability to turn a broken play into positive yardage. But there have been too many moments when he hesitates to make that decision as well. The Seahawks can put him in favorable situations. They can simplify his reads. They can use his legs as a designed part of the offense. Eventually, though, Milroe has to pull the trigger. That’s why I still expect Seattle to give him significant playing time against the Kansas City Chiefs. Based on how the Seahawks approached the previous preseason finale against the Green Bay Packers, the plan seemed to be giving Milroe as many reps as possible and allowing him to work through these situations. After what happened against the Titans, however, it will be interesting to see whether Seattle sticks with that plan. None of this means Milroe’s career is over. Quarterbacks sometimes take much longer than expected to figure things out. Malik Willis, for example, had a career defined more by lows than highs early on, moving from the Titans and eventually around the league before getting an opportunity to show more with the Packers. That eventually helped him earn a significant contract with the Dolphins last year. Geno Smith is an even better reminder of how unpredictable quarterback development can be. After years of struggles and opportunities that didn’t work out, he eventually put together a solid season and changed the trajectory of his career. Sam Darnold followed a similar path. He entered the NFL as the No. 3 overall pick after a strong run at USC and was widely considered a legitimate franchise quarterback prospect. Things didn’t work out with the Jets, and his career went through Carolina and San Francisco before he eventually found stability with the Vikings and later the Seahawks. Milroe doesn’t have anything close to Darnold’s draft pedigree or the same level of hype coming out of college. But that’s not really the point. The point is that quarterbacks can develop late. Milroe’s second season is not going to determine whether he can become an NFL starter. There are too many variables between now and then, and the Seahawks aren’t going to make a final judgment based on a couple of preseason games. But the clock does start moving. Drew Lock’s contract is set to expire after this season, while Sam Darnold enters the final year of his deal in 2027. The Seahawks will eventually have to decide whether to extend Darnold, bring in another quarterback or address the position through the draft. Milroe will be part of that equation. And that’s why this preseason matters, even if it isn’t definitive. The goal was never for Milroe to become a finished quarterback in August. The goal was to see progress. The goal was to see him close the gap on Lock, become more comfortable operating the offense and show the Seahawks that the enormous physical talent they invested in can eventually translate into quarterback play. So far, he hasn’t done enough of that. There is still plenty of time to change the narrative. But Milroe needs to start showing the Seahawks why they should keep believing in the project.
author: Alexandre Castro

title: Who was the biggest surprise of the preseason for the 49ers?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ preseason is officially over. The team will make roster decisions. The coaching staff should know by now who will make the team. Realistically, we’re talking about 3-5 spots up for grabs. Kyle Shanahan said he likes when players make it easy on him. Jacob Cowing did that with an 80+ yard […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: Jordan Watkins #17 of the San Francisco 49ers signals first down after catching a pass against the Tennessee Titans in the first half at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ preseason is officially over. The team will make roster decisions. The coaching staff should know by now who will make the team. Realistically, we’re talking about 3-5 spots up for grabs. Kyle Shanahan said he likes when players make it easy on him. Jacob Cowing did that with an 80+ yard punt return in the second preseason game. De’Zhaun Stribling’s roster spot was never in doubt, but he made an impact in both games. Defensively, Jack Jones had the ball production the 49ers so desperately covet at cornerback. He gave Raheem Morris confidence during the preseason. Now that the preseason is over, who surprised you? Who was the biggest surprise of the preseason for the 49ers? It’s always fun to read what people-watching practice is saying and then see for yourself how the players perform. In a practice setting, it’s easy to get caught up in one flashy play and ignore what happens on a down-to-down basis. That brings me to my answer. I have two: one pleasant surprise, and one…not so much. Jordan Watkins is the kind of player who has preseason production in the box score, but once you go under the hood and focus on him, I’m not sure he’s an NFL player. Not for the 49ers, at least. Football is a violent game. Unfortunately for Watkins, there were too many exposures during the preseason of him either shying away from contact or failing to produce through contact. If we use the final preseason game as an example, Watkins turtled up on his first kickoff return when he was about to get tackled. He had an opportunity to block a safety, but he waited and was driven back instead of being the aggressor. Then you get into tracking the ball in the air, and you’re left wondering whether Watkins is worth investing in, or if you should listen to the signs he’s telling you and move on. Kurtis Rourke only played in one game. He’s closer to Mac Jones than Adrian Martinez. It’s too bad that Rourke was banged up, because it would have been fun to see him grow over three weeks with extended reps. The good news is that we saw him drop back 16 times, and that was more than enough to see a quality backup. Half of Rourke’s completions went for first downs. He was selectively aggressive—which is another reason multiple games would have been fun, to see if Rourke would’ve opened it up even more. Rourke completed all four of his passes beyond 10 yards. The 32-yarder to Stribling on third down was a thing of beauty, and the type of aggressive decision Kyle Shanahan wants at the position. Rourke handled pressure well, and even avoided a sack. I thought he looked the part and wouldn’t dare think about losing him to waivers. Who surprised you the most this season?
author: Kyle Posey

title: 4 Winners and 2 losers: Is the 49ers’ defensive line depth good enough?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ preseason finale didn’t have a touchdown scored. The special teams showed out, while the rookies continued to learn on the fly as the coaching staff evaluated the roster. Let’s get into the final winners and losers from August. Winners Eddy Pineiro Kyle Shanahan said he was “pissed” at Pineiro for deferring […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Alfred Collins #95 of the San Francisco 49ers stands on the field with his teammates during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ preseason finale didn’t have a touchdown scored. The special teams showed out, while the rookies continued to learn on the fly as the coaching staff evaluated the roster. Let’s get into the final winners and losers from August. Winners Eddy Pineiro Kyle Shanahan said he was “pissed” at Pineiro for deferring to the second half in the preseason. The 49ers kicker followed that up with a touchback on the opening kick. You’re here to evaluate players covering kicks, so it was an 0-2 start for Pineiro. That would be his last blunder. Dineiro Pineiro made all six of his field goal attempts, including three from 50+ and a 59-yarder. The ball barely moved. Pineiro was making his kicks with room to spare. Corliss Waitman Waitman could end up being one of the better additions for the Niners this offseason, if his preseason performance is any indication. He had four punts with a net average of 46.5 yards. All four of his punts landed inside of the 20. Two of them were fair caught. The other two didn’t gain any yards. And Waitman’s long was 53 yards. Any time you can make your opponent go 80+ yards, you’ve done your job. Jack Jones Jones only played six snaps. He gave up a curl route for 14 yards. But he jumped a Brock Bowers route for a near interception. Those are the types of plays 49ers cornerbacks haven’t been in a position to make in several years. Jones also made an open-field tackle and was a willing run defender in limited action. Jones is a different type of player than what the Niners have had at cornerback in some time. That might end up being a good thing. Khalil Dinkins This kid is worth investing in. On Dinkins’ second play, the team trusted him to stay in and pass protect. He ended up helping right tackle Brandon Parker on a defensive lineman. On the next play, Dinkins drove the safety about seven yards from where he started. On the play where Jordan James ran for 17 yards, Dinkins worked to the linebacker and secured him, paving the way for James. Who knows if Dinkins ever turns into a viable pass catcher, but he is the exact type of prospect the team has drafted in the sixth round under this regime. Dinkins is a keeper. The aggression he plays with is palpable. Dinkins blocks with the intent that George Kittle would admire. He should stick on the practice squad. Losers The defensive line We did not see Sam Okuayinonu, Osa Odighizuwa, Nick Bosa, or Romello Height. So, the players who project to log starter snaps. Alfred Collins, a second-round pick, played late into the third quarter. Shanahan cited that it was because of rust. The reality is that Collins has not been effective. It was the same as it’s been in each of the previous two games for Collins. He was moved easily against the run and did not win as a pass rusher. I’d argue the best run play from a defensive tackle was by Keion White on third down. Outside of that, Collins, CJ West, Sebastian Davis, James Thompson Jr., and Bryson Eason all left a lot to be desired against the Raiders’ first- and second-team offensive line. They made Spencer Burford look good. Nobody really won when it came to rushing the passer, either. Ogbo Okoronkwo had a couple of pressures, but no other defensive lineman can say the same. West won once as a pass rusher. So did Thompson Jr. and Valdez. But that does it as far as wins are concerned. It was an uninspiring performance from a group that had given us hope during the past couple of weeks. Maybe this is who they are, and it’s a sign the 49ers need to add bodies who are not on the roster in an effort to find somebody who can contribute while Mykel Williams is out. The defensive line depth, unsurprisingly, is concerning. Carver Willis Willis may win the left guard job because nobody else around him can stay healthy. But it won’t be because of the product he put out in the preseason after Week 1. Willis is inconsistent, as you’d expect from a rookie. He played the entire first half. In those 29 snaps, it’s problematic if Willis is going against a defensive tackle with length. He still looks unsure of who to block at times when on the move. But I think his ability to strain blocks, aka hold his ground when he’s head up against somebody 1-on-1, could be an issue. I think Willis will end up being a good player, but it’s obvious he needs some time. Can the 49ers afford to give him that time?
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 stars from the 49ers preseason finale: The depth at running back looks better than ever
summary: The third preseason game is usually the dress rehearsal for the regular season, but with a trip across the world looming, Kyle Shanahan decided to see what roster spots 23-53 look like to close the preseason. While the Las Vegas Raiders went with their starters, Thursday turned into a kicking battle, with Eddy Pineiro outdueling […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 20: Kaelon Black #26 of the San Francisco 49ers rushes during the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. The 49ers defeated the Chargers 41-17. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The third preseason game is usually the dress rehearsal for the regular season, but with a trip across the world looming, Kyle Shanahan decided to see what roster spots 23-53 look like to close the preseason. While the Las Vegas Raiders went with their starters, Thursday turned into a kicking battle, with Eddy Pineiro outdueling Matt Gay and leading the 49ers to an 18-12 victory. Had this been a regular-season game, Pineiro would have been a runaway for the No. 1 star, but with him already a lock for the roster, let’s look at three players who used the preseason finale to earn a job and/or earn a spot on the initial 53-man roster. These are the three stars as the 49ers close the book on the preseason and look forward to Melbourne: 3rd Star – RB Kaelon Black/RB Jordan James The 49ers are set at running back. It might not matter with Christian McCaffrey taking the lion’s share of the carries in the regular season, but the depth is there. Both Black and James looked the part as neither blew up the box score, but both certainly passed the eye test. The duo combined for 63 yards on 12 attempts, with both recording impressive runs during their reps. Black got the first look on Thursday, looking to build off his impressive debut last week. While he didn’t get too many chances, just four carries, Black made the most of them, averaging seven yards per attempt, closing his day with 28 rushing yards. A bulk of those 28 yards came on one run. With the 49ers deep in Las Vegas territory following a Fernando Mendoza interception, the 49ers wanted to get Black involved early. He would take the opening carry around the right edge and show an impressive speed boost to get the corner and turn upfield for a gain of 14. Shanahan seemed impressed enough to make that Black’s final touch of the evening. James entered from there and got chances early. On his first drive, he was fed the ball on three straight plays, gaining nine on the first two plays before losing a yard on third down, forcing a San Francisco punt. But James would turn it on from there. It would start with a quick 20-yard reception that would move the 49ers into plus territory. A few plays later, James would get his big play, exploding through the line for a gain of 17, leading to another Pineiro field goal. Black and James were already locks to make the initial 53-man, but seeing what they look like sharing the backfield gives plenty of confidence to a backup running back spot that’s had plenty of turnover in recent years. 2nd Star – LG Carver Willis The 49ers have treated the left guard spot like a carousel over training camp and the preseason, with Connor Colby and Robert Jones getting first looks before Austen Pleasants got a look last week. It was Willis’s turn this week and he might not give up the spot. Willis played the entire first half without being noticed too much, which is probably a good thing for an offensive lineman trying to earn a spot on the starting line. While Willis was on the field, the 49ers didn’t allow a single sack. And while that’s an accomplishment for the entire line, Willis also didn’t allow a single pressure according to Pro Football Focus. It might have been a very backwards way to find a starting left guard, but Willis’s performance on Thursday might have done the trick to find an answer to the more infuriating question of 49ers training camp. 1st Star – LB Tatum Bethune/LB Jaden Dugger With the 49ers acquiring Deion Jones earlier this week, the 49ers have about eight linebackers with a case to make the roster. Last year, the 49ers kept five linebackers on the initial 53-man, but the year before they kept six, so eight players for either five or six spots. Obviously, somebody is going to miss out. Dugger seemed like a sure thing to make the roster, especially with his versatility to play the defensive line. He made a strong final impression against the Raiders, leading the 49ers with 10 tackles and hit the Raiders quarterback twice. Sure, there was a bad missed tackle to stop what would turn out to be a Las Vegas third-down, but overall it was a solid performance from the rookie who has proved he could be used in a vital role this season for a somewhat rebuilt San Francisco defense. If there was one player who stood out as much as Dugger on Thursday night, it would be Bethune. Bethune entered Thursday night more on the fringe than Dugger, which might make his game slightly more impressive. Only Dugger finished with more tackles than Bethune, who finished with nine tackles, but Bethune was more present in the passing game, recording a pass breakup and finding himself in the right spot at the right time to intercept Mendoza in the first quarter. Two impressive performances, one from a rookie who’s looking to earn a role in the NFL, and one on the roster bubble. We will see how the 53-man roster looks come Sunday, but it was an emphatic final performance from both Bethune and Dugger.
author: Andrew Pasquini

His decisiveness shown on a 3rd & 1 run last week ended up being a mistake Jordan James made in his first action. Black gave way to James in the second quarter. On a 3rd & 1 run, James attempted to cut against the grain instead of staying on his path and picking up the first down. That’s a good learning moment for James. James broke a run himself. He had a 17-yarder and also took a screen pass 20 yards. James isn’t flashy, but he’s the type of back to bounce off tackles and fall forward for a few extra yards. That’s what you want in a backup. He’ll learn to stick his nose in there and maximize the yardage in short-yardage situations… …The most intriguing rookie may have been undrafted free agent tight end Khalil Dinkins. He’s listed at 6’4”, 226 pounds. That might be about 15 pounds too light. He played blocked with a level of intensity in limited action that is worth keeping around on the practice squad.” Why is 49ers’ Carver Willis getting another start at LG? The rookie needs the reps (paywall) “Outsiders tend to fixate on pass protection when evaluating offensive linemen. The 49ers, however, scrutinize run blocking, especially following a season in which the team’s per-carry average, a robust 4.52 yards in the first eight seasons under Shanahan, dropped to 3.78 yards. It was the first time in his tenure the average fell below 4 yards. Willis emphasized that the 49ers’ run-blocking scheme is an extremely precise choreography — a Chorus Line but with 315-pound defensive tackles trying to blow up the performance. His biggest issue right now is that he’s slightly out of step. Or in his words: “My angles in the run game aren’t very complementary of the guys next to me.” A false step by the left guard on a running play isn’t something a casual observer usually picks up on, but it is obvious — like a sour note during a piano recital — to an expert like offensive line coach Chris Foerster. “There are so many plays where you can see that the four guys next to me — their hips are on a different angle than mine,” Willis said. “For me right now, it’s studying that aiming point and running on our angles, setting our backside shoulder, all that kind of stuff.” One benefit to playing left guard for the 49ers, he said, is that he has Trent Williams, who’s played 11,334 career snaps, to his left and Jake Brendel (4,376 career snaps) to the right. And that means he often gets real-time coaching in the huddle. “Those guys have been so great,” Willis said. “They’ll tell you when you did well. Be like, ‘Hey, great job on that. That’s exactly what we need.’ Or it’s, ‘Hey, come on. You have to see that quicker.’ Or, ‘You’ve got to get hands on the guy.’ I’ve got a combined 23 years of experience next to me. That’s huge. Our vets have been so helpful.” Will 49ers trust Kaelon Black, Jordan James enough to lighten Christian McCaffrey’s load? (Paywall) “Thursday night was James’ only chance to put something on tape ahead of the season opener in Australia. And he looked good for the most part. James finished with 35 yards on eight carries, including a 17-yarder up the gut with good contact balance, along with a 20-yard catch, which was a screen pass that turned into much more upon his cutback and a nice perimeter block by rookie left guard hopeful Carver Willis. His momentary lapses: Running sideways instead of vertical on a third-and-1 carry that lost a yard (one Black would probably convert) and getting flagged for an illegal block that negated a touchdown pass.”

title: 49ers waiver wire: What position are the 49ers in, and what players are subject to the process?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers just finished up their final preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders and now will be scrambling to make final roster cuts to the 53-man roster. We say scrambling because the team needs to get on a plane to Melbourne, Australia, to play the Los Angeles Rams in Week 1. With […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch enters the field prior to a preseason NFL football game against the Tennessee Titans at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers just finished up their final preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders and now will be scrambling to make final roster cuts to the 53-man roster. We say scrambling because the team needs to get on a plane to Melbourne, Australia, to play the Los Angeles Rams in Week 1. With that in mind, they need to figure out who is and isn’t going so they can make travel arrangements. Over at FanDuel Sportsbook , the 49ers are currently sitting as 3.5-point underdogs in their game against the Rams. Since the game is in Australia, not in San Francisco or Los Angeles, it’s safe to say many of those odds were initially set based on the rosters. While the 49ers are a bit more urgent, all NFL teams will be trimming their rosters from 90 to 53 in the coming days. The deadline to have a 53-man roster is Sunday, August 30 at 3:00 PM PST . Those cut are either released outright or waived—depending on their time in the league. There are a few wrinkles in 2026 the 49ers can take advantage of. First is IR. If a player is placed on IR, two players can be tagged as designated to return and can come back after missing at least four games. Teams must tag a player in this category, however. They can’t pick and choose players later in the season after putting them on IR months earlier. Any other players placed on IR (READ: Ricky Pearsall) are done for the year. Then there’s the physically unable to perform or PUP list. If a player is on this list, it means they were placed on it before the season began. The moment they practice or play in even a preseason game, they are off the PUP list. Any players on PUP are subject to the same four-game minimum as one on IR. The difference is that PUP players didn’t practice or play in the preseason. Players with at least four years of experience are released and become unrestricted free agents. They can go anywhere and sign with any team. No restrictions. Those under the four-year threshold are subject to waivers and the waiver wire. The following players have been, or are associated with, the 49ers’ 90-man roster this year and are subject to waivers: QB Kurtis Rourke QB Adrian Martinez RB Kaelon Black RB Jordan James RB Sincere McCormick WR De’Zhaun Stribling WR Jacob Cowing WR Jordan Watkins WR Wesley Grimes WR Will Pauling TE Brayden Willis TE Hayden Rucci TE Khalil Dinkins OG Dominick Puni OG Connor Colby OL Carver Willis OL Drake Nugent OL Enrique Cruz Jr. OL Isaac Alarcon DL Romello Height DL Alfred Collins DL Gracen Halton DL CJ West DL Sebastian Valdez DL James Thompson Jr. DL Bryson Eason DL Evan Anderson LB Jaden Dugger LB Tatum Bethune LB Nick Martin LB Larry Worth III CB Renardo Green CB Upton Stout CB Ephesians Prysock CB Jakob Robinson S Malik Mustapha S Patrick McMorris S Marques Sigle S Jalen Stroman On waivers, teams can claim players, but the order is determined by the draft order from earlier this year. The 49ers picked 27 (or at least their pick was 27, since they traded it to the Miami Dolphins), so they will be the 27th team to make a selection. So if there’s any player on waivers they want, then they have to wait for 26 other teams to decide they don’t want that specific player. Any team that makes a waiver claim must open a roster spot to keep the roster at 53 players. If the player is claimed, another player is waived/released in return. Also, this isn’t like fantasy football; a team can’t place four waiver claims in order of importance and get only one before things switch to the next team. Any team can make multiple claims, and if they’re ahead of the 49ers, they can get all the players the 49ers may want—provided the team has opened roster spots for those players. That means the Las Vegas Raiders and New York Jets can be much more active on the waiver wire than the Seattle Seahawks, who go last due to winning the Super Bowl. The current waiver order is as follows: Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville Jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills San Francisco 49ers Houston Texans Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks The 49ers have a lot of waiting to do if they want any hot players that couldn’t fit on any of the teams before them. That said, the teams before them need to do a lot of roster reshuffling. The one thing to take from all of this is that the 53-man roster you see on Monday isn’t going to be the same 53-man roster you see on Tuesday or Wednesday. Or Monday a couple hours later.

title: 49ers listed among the least watchable teams heading into 2026
summary: The San Francisco 49ers won in 2025, but they weren’t what’d you call a sight for sore eyes. It was worse in 2024. We’re two years removed from a 2023 season that was one of the most aesthetically pleasing years of any team in the NFL. Everything came easy offensively. Kyle Shanahan is hoping that’s […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - FEBRUARY 11: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates a defensive stop with Dre Greenlaw #57 during the first half against the Kansas City Chiefs during Super Bowl LVIII at Allegiant Stadium on February 11, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers won in 2025, but they weren’t what’d you call a sight for sore eyes. It was worse in 2024. We’re two years removed from a 2023 season that was one of the most aesthetically pleasing years of any team in the NFL. Everything came easy offensively. Kyle Shanahan is hoping that’s Brock Purdy’s life in 2026. It’ll be the best supporting cast for Purdy since ‘23. He has a legitimate WR1. And unlike in years past, Purdy has a pair of wide receivers who thrive in contested situations. The depth in the backfield should make Christian McCaffrey better. Kaelon Black and Jordan James should be sneaky good contributors, and not just in 2026. If the 49ers can find a left guard who can hold his own, the offense has a chance to be special. ESPN’s Benjamin Solak compiled a watchability list , ranking every team based on quality offenses, star players, competitive games, and explosive plays. Surprisingly, the 49ers checked in low on the list. They were 20th, one spot below the Colts and one spot in front of the Panthers: The 49ers under coach Kyle Shanahan — so long as the offense is decently healthy — have always been pleasantly view-worthy. Even a quarterback injury can’t slow Shanahan down — those early-season Mac Jones games in 2025 were hilariously fun. Even as running back Christian McCaffrey , now 30, diminishes in athleticism and tight end George Kittle returns from a right Achilles tear , I’ll believe in a bad 49ers offense only when I see it, and not a moment before. San Francisco played in only six one-score games last season — fewer than any other team — thanks in large part to a porous defense that was among the bottom 10 in most metrics. Fortunately for the Niners, bad defense and good offense can make for surprisingly watchable games. Take their Week 16 primetime game against the Colts in December. It was the only watchable Philip Rivers game after he came out of retirement to be Indianapolis’ quarterback at 44 years old … and it was because the 49ers’ defense was shaky enough to make it so. The 49ers should be healthier on both sides of the ball this season, so they might just be a boring version of pleasantly good. But 25% of their games are against NFC West rivals, the Rams and Seahawks, and those contests always deliver. If August has taught us anything, it’s that the 49ers will not be boring. The defense will be somewhat of a wildcard. The front four will be the deepest it’s been in some time. Osa Odighizuwa is still a move that is flying under the radar — Solak didn’t even mention him. Role players like Sam Okuayinonu and Keion White won’t need to be overextended. Having your two best players, Nick Bosa and Fred Warner, takes pressure off the other nine players on the field.
author: Kyle Posey

Dimukeje signed with the team on August 17 . Joyner gives the Niners a Dimukeje replacement for tonight’s game. The 49ers working out a pass rusher the day before their preseason finale makes sense. Because of that, you don’t run the risk of the players you believe will play in Week 1 playing in a meaningless game for them two weeks before the season kicks off. Romello Height has an ankle injury he’s been nursing . The 49ers will give Height as long as he needs to get as close to 100% as he can ahead of Week 1. Height played 18 and 13 snaps in the first two preseason games. The 49ers probably would have liked to see their rookie get a few more live game reps ahead of Week 1 had it not been for an injury. It’s another reason to host Height’s position for a tryout. That was the only transaction, which suggests the team didn’t sign Joyner and is content with the rotation they can field with their current roster. We’ll provide any updates if that changes. Heading into Thursday night, with Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, and Keion White projected out, the other edge rushers are Quinton Bell, Ogbo Okoronkwo, and Villiami Fehoko Jr. Sam Okuayinonu is on track to start. He’s Mykel’s replacement as an early-down run defender. Sam O is not a player you can risk with an injury. I wouldn’t expect to see him on Thursday.

title: Commanders preseason: Ricky Barber among players to watch vs. Ravens
summary: Most Commanders you’ll see featured during the 2026 campaign won’t play Friday night’s preseason finale against Baltimore.   Head coach Dan Quinn made that crystal clear this week, saying frontline players would get heavy reps in Wednesday’s joint practice against the Ravens to cap their training camp.   That means the cast you see Friday […]
full_text: Most Commanders you’ll see featured during the 2026 campaign won’t play Friday night’s preseason finale against Baltimore. Head coach Dan Quinn made that crystal clear this week, saying frontline players would get heavy reps in Wednesday’s joint practice against the Ravens to cap their training camp. That means the cast you see Friday at M&T Bank Stadium will feature those battling for spots near the bottom of the 53-man depth chart and the practice squad. That doesn’t mean this upcoming game is without merit, though you must look a little harder to find it. Most of the hay’s in the barn evaluation-wise, but finishing with a flourish may help some roster hopefuls secure a spot. Notice how you don’t see quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis or defensive back Tyler Owens listed. I think those guys are already in. There are a few players worth highlighting here that could improve their stock and standing by punctuating the preseason with a strong performance. DL Ricky Barber A first-year pro after spending most of last season on the practice squad, Ricky Barber has shown well during training camp. That’s also true of his preseason performances. While the Commanders vastly upgraded their defensive front, Johnny Newton’s torn pectoral muscle has created an opening for a young player like Barber. He leads the team with 10 tackles and a sack over the first two preseason games, and was solid when elevated from the practice squad in 2025, especially on this play. Ricky Barber's first career NFL sack. The UDFA rookie from UCF has been waiting for his opportunity to play all season. pic.twitter.com/dasUXczJ35 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) December 25, 2025 Barber surely has a practice-squad spot locked up, unless someone snags him off waivers, where he could provide insurance at the position. Barber could earn a spot should the Commanders keep six defensive linemen, though Byron Cowart’s angling for the same gig. A strong finish could help Barber in this instance, to highlight a strong body of preseason work. DB Darius Rush Credit where credit’s due: This one’s inspired by John Portis’ excellent roster case for Darius Rush, a supreme athlete and special teams maven who clearly cares about the kicking game. A team needs players like that, to champion the often thankless work done on the coverage and return units. Darius Rush with a great special teams tackle pic.twitter.com/nVkl7lSg4J — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 15, 2026 Two red zone opportunities for rookie Ja'Kobi Lane. Two incompletions. pic.twitter.com/avY8MY5zLc — Sam Cohn (@samdcohn) August 26, 2026 Showing a little something on defensive coverage in the preseason, even if it’s the tools to develop into a solid player in that area, will strengthen his case to be kept around in Washington. He might not make the 53-man roster, but he could well help this season as a practice squad elevation and continue to earn reps with hard work. LB Ale Kaho Ale Kaho has had a strong preseason, showing off the athleticism and special-teams prowess worthy of a reserve linebacker spot. Ale Kaho with the INT! Nice drop by Ale, but the pressure up front caused this. pic.twitter.com/hEeikyD29A — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 It seems like the Commanders like Kaho and have him under strong consideration should they keep a fifth linebacker as I think they will. Fellow UCLA product Kain Medrano ’s direct competition for that spot and he’s an Adam Peters draft pick with somewhat similar traits. It’s tough to say who has the upper hand at this point – probably Medrano – and this is the type of competition that could go to the bitter end even with most decisions already made. A final evaluation could further prove his worth, though it’s nearly impossible he won’t earn a practice squad spot at minimum. WR Jaden Bradley The undrafted rookie out of UNLV has been talked about a ton over the course of this Commanders preseason, with mostly positive sentiments from players, coaches and observers alike. I mean, what’s not to love about a hard worker who makes plays like this? Jaden Bradley getting arm-barred and still making the one-handed catch! pic.twitter.com/iUCFJd66v3 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 22, 2026 His play would put him in line for a roster spot on this team, but that’s hard to imagine in an impacted position group. There are times, however, when teams take a flier on a young player with upside who plays special teams over a veteran with a defined ceiling. Could more wow plays against the Ravens sway general manager Adam Peters to keep Bradley on the 53-man roster. Could Washington get him through waivers and onto the practice squad? Probably, but it’s a risk. Maybe he’s on the initial 53-man and gets moved a week or so later. There’s so much worthy competition for the sixth receiver spot, but Bradley has a case he can keep on making Friday night. OT D.J. Humphries This player doesn’t fit the theme we’ve created for this post. Humphries is an established veteran, albeit towards the end of a standout career. He made it clear to on-site reporters following Wednesday’s joint practice that he’s not a savior at the left tackle spot. He’s here to provide depth behind Brandon Coleman. This game will offer a sneak peek of what Humphries can do at this stage, with but a small amount of scheme knowledge under his belt. Keep an eye on his game reps – there might not be many – for an indication of where he’s at after spending most of camp away from an NFL team.

Commanders links all squared away @CarterMachinery | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/rADCbxW6TB — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 28, 2026 Articles Sports Illustrated 5 Questions Commanders Still Must Answer Before Final Roster Cuts 3. How Many Running Backs Can Washington Keep? The running back room became a lot more interesting once the preseason started. Jacory Croskey-Merritt showed up to camp with more muscle and ready to compete, but he has what Dan Quinn has described as a lower-body issue that he’s working through. Kaytron Allen has continued strengthening his case , while Robert Henry Jr. went from being an afterthought in most roster projections to somebody Washington has to seriously consider after his performance against Miami. Jeremy McNichols looked fairly secure as the veteran fourth back entering camp before a quadriceps injury removed him from several important late-preseason opportunities. Washington then signed veteran Craig Reynolds , initially because the team simply needed another healthy running back to get through practices and games. Still, every additional body adds another option. The decision here can’t be made strictly by looking at rushing totals either. Pass protection, special teams, third-down reliability, and which backs can actually be active on game day will matter. Allen and Henry have made this a much harder decision than it seemed a month ago, and Washington now has to decide whether the young backs have done enough to change the original roster math. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Why Athan Kaliakmanis should replace Sam Hartman on the Commanders roster Kaliakmanis has completed 17 of 24 passes for 249 yards, averaging 10.38 yards per attempt with zero interceptions and an aggregate passer rating that reflects a quarterback playing with confidence rather than just managing the game. His 10.38 yards per attempt is elite by any standard — in the regular season, that number would rank among the best in the NFL. It’s preseason, yes. But the traits it reflects — arm talent, intermediate accuracy, downfield aggressiveness, comfort in the pocket — don’t disappear when the games start counting. The scheme fit matters too. David Blough’s offense is built on play-action, RPOs, and rollouts that require a quarterback who can plant and drive the ball downfield from unconventional platforms. Kaliakmanis looks more comfortable after two preseason games than Hartman has in three years of being in the building. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Mailbag: Bill and a roster long shot (or two) Do you feel Jacory Croskey-Merritt has improved his pass blocking enough this offseason to warrant more snaps on third downs? I would say so, and it’s arguably what has stood out the most about Croskey-Merritt, who had a good camp. His struggles in that area were one of the reasons he received fewer carries in the middle of last season, despite his abilities with the ball in his hands. There’s more to being an NFL running back than carrying the ball; it’s something that every rookie player at the position must learn. I don’t think he was ever unwilling to pass block, but learning the proper techniques and physical requirements can take time. Croskey-Merritt has put his full effort into improving that area of his skill set, and it has shown up on the field. That’s going to get him more snaps on the field, and if fans have shown anything over the past year, it’s that they love when they see Bill in the lineup. Who’s your long shots for making the season-opening 53? The one that comes to my mind is Antonio Hamilton Sr. He has such a good story being an 11-year veteran who has bounced around the league. He was with the Commanders last year and performed well in spot duty. He does have some length to his frame, but what really makes him stand out is his energy and enthusiasm. He gives his all on every play, and that kind of effort matters to coaches. If he does make the team, it would likely be mostly for special teams purposes, but players like Hamilton are welcome in that unit. I have no idea how many cornerbacks they plan to keep, but if they do keep five, it wouldn’t surprise me if he was one of them. I think you could make the same case for Ale Kaho . To read more of this article, CLICK HERE A to Z Sports Washington Commanders’ new offense could unlock the best version of Jayden Daniels yet “Get a quarterback under center. Gives you so many different looks, throws a defense off,” Anderson said. “It’s not just sitting in the pistol knowing that it’s one of three plays that’s going to happen.” Anderson noted that early reports out of training camp suggest the offense is not coming together quickly, which he views as a positive sign rather than a negative one. A longer installation process should keep defenses off balance over the full 17-game slate. Washington needs variance to avoid the Miami trap The biggest risk for Blough’s offense is falling into a predictable pattern. Anderson pointed to the Miami Dolphins’ timing-based attack under coach Mike McDaniel as a cautionary tale. That system was easily dissolved once defenses realized it ran the same concepts out of the same three formations, requiring defenders only to fill three predetermined spots to shut it down. Washington cannot afford to be one-dimensional. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Pro Football Talk Commanders’ online store sells out of merchandise with old name and logo Controversial or not, there’s an appetite for merchandise with the Commanders’ outdated name and logo. Via Eric Flack of WUSA, who first reported on the sale of gear bearing the abandoned name and logo earlier this week, all items featuring the old logo and name at the team’s online store have sold out . Per Flack, items remain available at the team’s brick-and-mortar store. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN 2026 NFL season: Ranking all 32 teams’ watchability, excitement 13. Washington Commanders The Commanders were my most watchable team entering 2025 off Jayden Daniels ‘ uproarious Offensive Rookie of the Year season, penchant for close games (they won on multiple Hail Mary plays, remember) and a high pace of play that made for a lot more football. Of course, I didn’t calculate absolutely everyone getting hurt — but that’s on me. Daniels was must-see television in 2024 and, in a new offense, should get back to that form in 2026. No quarterback scrambles more often than Daniels (16.0% last season). The new defensive approach under coordinator Daronte Jones, hired from the Brian Flores tree, should be aggressive and creative. So, we should see more big plays for the defense and the offense. Plus, with head coach Dan Quinn starting the season on the hot seat, the stakes should be high in early-season games.
