title: Washington Commanders 91-man 2026 preseason Game 3 roster/depth chart
summary: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this […]
full_text: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this IPP exemption, as they have again this season, so Washington’s offseason roster limit is once again 91 players. Washington’s 91st player via the IPP is currently edge rusher TJ Maguranyanga , who spent the 2025 season on the Commanders roster. Surprising number of roster changes since the Lions game In the four days that followed the Lions game, the Commanders announced nine roster moves. Released/Waived (3) RB Jerome Ford (released from IR with injury settlement) The veteran running back will have the opportunity to sign with any of the other 31 NFL teams if he is healthy, but, per the NFL CBA, cannot play for the Commanders in 2026. This move did not affect the number of players on the roster since Ford, on IR, was not counted against the 91-man limit. S Will Harris After entering spring OTAs as one of the presumed starting safeties, Harris was released after the Lions game, presumably to give him the opportunity to catch on with another NFL roster ahead of Sunday’s mass cutdowns. OT Foster Sarell Sarell was released in conjunction with the signing of OT D.J. Humphries, which is simply an attempt by the Commanders to upgrade the position group. Injured Reserve (2) When a player is placed on injured reserve during training camp, he is ineligible to return to play for the team that season although he can subsequently be waived with an injury settlement and play for another team when healthy. S Malik Spencer The undrafted free agent was expected by many to wind up on the Commanders practice squad. The rookie safety was waived with an injury designation (hamstring) on Tuesday. Because he went unclaimed by another NFL team, he officially cleared waivers and reverted back to Washington’s roster the following day. As explained above, he will either spend the 2026 season on IR with Washington, or he can be released later with an injury settlement, and will be free to sign with any other NFL team. He cannot take the field in a regular or postseason game for the Commanders in 2026. EDGE Drake Jackson Jackson, who has lost past seasons due to issues with his patellar tendon, reportedly injured his hamstring during training camp/preseason work. A quick NFL Rules Tutorial: One potential benefit to players of being placed on IR in preseason Accrued Seasons vs. Credited Seasons Credited and Accrued season are important to NFL players: Credited Season (3 Games): Used strictly for player benefits (pension, 401k, life insurance). Accrued Season (6 Games): Used to earn time toward free agency milestones. What happens if a player is placed on IR during the preseason? Automatic Benefit: If a player is placed on IR in the preseason and remains on IR for the first three weeks of the regular season , he will automatically accrue a credited season . A player on IR must remain on full-pay status for at least six regular-season games to earn an accrued season . The Exception (Injury Settlements): If the team negotiates an injury settlement and releases the player during the preseason, he only gets a credited season if the financial settlement covers the equivalent of three or more regular-season game checks; if the settlement covers at least six, he qualifies for an accrued season. Credited seasons are more likely to be of importance to marginal players — especially those with very short careers or who spend a lot of time moving on and off of team rosters and practice squads — as player benefits are often tied to credited seasons. Some things that are likely to interest fans, such as a player’s minimum salary, are based on credited seasons rather than accrued seasons. For a player who might have been cut without ever making the team’s roster , being placed on IR during the preseason could potentially help that player add a credited or accrued season, enhancing his qualification for benefits or moving him a year closer to unrestricted free agency. Signed (4) OT D.J. Humphries Humphries spent nine seasons with the Cardinals (2015–2023), establishing himself as a premium blindside protector and earning a Pro Bowl selection in 2021. He accumulated 101 career NFL starts. Following a torn ACL near the end of 2023, he became a journeyman backup. Humphries played two games for the Kansas City Chiefs in 2024 and appeared in eight regular-season games for the Los Angeles Rams in 2025. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn made it clear that he would provide depth behind Brandon Coleman as opposed to taking over the starting LT position. OLB Boogie Basham Over five seasons, he has played in 43 career games as a rotational pass rusher , bouncing between the Buffalo Bills, New York Giants and Carolina Panthers. Before signing with Washington, he spent the first half of 2026 playing locally in the UFL for the DC Defenders, where he recorded 24 tackles and three sacks. S Joshua Bledsoe A 6th-round pick in 2021 , he spent his first three NFL seasons (2021–2023) with New England, appearing in four regular-season games primarily as a special teams contributor. Since leaving the Patriots, he has spent time on the offseason rosters or practice squads of the Pittsburgh Steelers and Tennessee Titans, and also spent time in the UFL with the San Antonio Brahmas. S Quindell Johnson After going undrafted in 2023, he was signed by the Los Angeles Rams and later claimed by the Chicago Bears. He appeared in nine regular-season NFL games with Chicago during his rookie year, recording two tackles and one interception. He also spent time with the San Francisco 49ers and Pittsburgh Steelers. Accounting for Laremy Tunsil & Johnny Newton While today’s chart lists 91 players, we know already that two of those players, LT Laremy Tunsil and DL Johnny Newton , will not be on the active roster in Week 1. Timing counts for a lot with players who suffer major injuries in training camp. Here’s a quick explanation of the considerations for placing a player on IR under the relevant NFL rules: 1. The Pre-Cutdown Rule (Season-Ending) As mentioned above, if the Commanders place Tunsil or Newton on IR during training camp before the final 53-man roster reduction deadline on Aug. 30, the player is automatically ruled out for the entire season . He would not be allowed to practice or play for Washington at any point during the year. While Tunsil and Newton have already undergone surgery, head coach Dan Quinn said that doctors have not yet determined the recovery timeline for either player. If doctors determine, in the coming days, that Tunsil and/or Newton will not be able to return to play prior to mid-February, then the Commanders might choose to exercise this option. 2. The Cutdown Day Exception (Designated to Return) NFL rules allow teams: a. to designate, on cutdown day (Aug 30th), up to two injured players to return from IR during the season. b. alternatively, the team can carry a player onto the initial 53-man roster and move him to IR the following day (Aug 31st) or later, opening up a roster spot; the only reason to do this would be if the team needed to designate two other players to return at the time the initial roster was set on Aug 30. (Option A is almost certainly the one that the Commanders would choose in Tunsil’s case, probably Newton as well) This approach (either option a or b) allows the player (Tunsil/Newton/both) to keep his season alive, as it leaves the door open for him to return after sitting out a minimum of four games (obviously, in these two cases, it would be closer to four months than four games). If doctors determine that the player’s (Tunsil’s/Newton’s/both) return to play could happen prior to mid-February, then the Commanders might choose this option to keep all possibilities on the…

title: Washington Commanders roster: Three potential trade candidates
summary: Commanders general manager Adam Peters won’t sleep much throughout this weekend. There’s an initial 53-man roster to form and a practice squad to construct, plus a waiver wire to scour for pieces that can help Washington as the 2026 regular season kicks off.   We previously mentioned the prospect of trading for an experienced reserve center, […]
full_text: Commanders general manager Adam Peters won’t sleep much throughout this weekend. There’s an initial 53-man roster to form and a practice squad to construct, plus a waiver wire to scour for pieces that can help Washington as the 2026 regular season kicks off. We previously mentioned the prospect of trading for an experienced reserve center , maybe someone losing a position battle who has more of a chance to contribute in Washington. Peters could secure a coveted player before he hits the open market with some Day 3 NFL draft capital. The Commanders need to pick up players, but they could also deal from positions of strength. While player-for-player deals are relatively rare in the NFL, Peters could acquire some assets or fortify weaknesses in trade. Washington has some tough choices ahead at receiver and linebacker especially, possibly with players who will get picked up on the waiver wire after getting cut. Understand that you’ve got to give up something to get something, which is why this list is short and the players on it must be attractive additions to another team. Here are a few options Peters could flip for an asset. WR Dyami Brown Dyami Brown has had a strong camp, especially of late, yet sits squarely on the roster bubble in a deep receiver group. The Stefon Diggs signing changed this position group, bumping those seemingly competing for prominent roles deeper on the depth chart. Return ability is a factor here as well, which is why Jaylin Lane and (to a lesser extent) Luke McCaffrey seem safe. That puts Brown and Treylon Burks in a bout for the No. 6 receiver spot – keeping seven doesn’t seem likely – and could make one of them a trade target. Brown could fetch a bit more considering his speed and consistent availability, and Burks is a big-play option who provides injury protection and a big-body in the pattern. Washington could trade Brown and be okay. LB Jordan Magee Jordan Magee seems set to make the 53-man roster as a solid reserve behind Sonny Styles, Frankie Luvu and Leo Chenal. The Commanders also have Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho, athletic linebackers and special teams contributors who have played well this preseason yet sit on the roster bubble. While Magee has dealt with shoulder problems during camp, he might be more attractive as a solid backup. Washington could survive with Medrano and Kaho if they moved Magee, but the return would have to be fair. EDGE Dorance Armstrong This seems more like a trade deadline deal prospect than something before the season, with Dorance Armstrong coming off a torn ACL while facing a one-game suspension to start the season. The Commanders have received solid early returns from rookie Joshua Josephs – he’s definitely still developing – and Javontae Jean-Baptiste. Amstrong is an excellent depth piece with tons of experience and injury protection at a premium position, but he’s in a contract year and might be deemed a valuable trade asset closer to the deadline after he has proven productive coming off of injury. Still, sometimes you must give something valuable to get something. Who else would you trade prior to final cuts for a center or to accumulate future draft capital? Let us know in the comments below.
author: Scott Bair

title: How every 2026 NFL draft pick has looked in the preseason
summary: When will Fernando Mendoza start? Should we expect big things for Sonny Styles, Ja'Kobi Lane and Cashius Howell? We checked in on all 32 NFL teams' rookie classes.
full_text:
The NFL's cut-down deadline is Sunday, and the 2026 NFL season  is less than two weeks away. But before 32 NFL rosters get pared down to 53 players  each, we're doing our annual inventory of the most recent draft class through training camp.

 We asked our NFL Nation writers to size up how all 257 draftees have fared since being selected. They have updates on every player who went off the board, from No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza to Broncos linebacker Red Murdock , this year's " Mr. Irrelevant ." Who is in line to start for their team? Who is outplaying their draft position in the preseason and could make an early impact? And which high picks are falling behind?

 Rookies are grouped by team below, and each team is listed in the order by which it made its first selection in April. That means we begin with the Raiders' class, before hitting the Jets and Cardinals and so on.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 

 
 

 Las Vegas Raiders 
 Round 1 (No. 1): Fernando Mendoza , QB.  Mendoza might not be the Week 1 starter, but signs of him being a franchise quarterback are there. Throughout training camp, players and coaches have praised the Heisman Trophy winner's improved confidence. He's unafraid of targeting tight windows. On top of that, he has a firmer grasp of the system, resulting in better command of the offense. "That's hard to do as a young guy," center Tyler Linderbaum said. "You're dealing with a lot of new things, a whole new offense. So seeing the growth in his command and operation, it's a good starting point."

 Round 2 (No. 38): Treydan Stukes , S. Stukes has picked up momentum lately. He performed well against the Texans in the second preseason game and played mostly with the first-team defense during the final week of training camp.

 Round 3 (No. 67): Keyron Crawford , edge rusher. Crawford has flashed at times during training camp while working mostly with the second-team defense. He's currently behind Maxx Crosby , Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce , but the Raiders like to rotate their edge rushers in games. So Crawford should get some playing time this season.

 Round 3 (No. 91): Trey Zuhn III , G/OT. The Raiders view Zuhn as an interior offensive lineman, but he has played right tackle in preseason games. It seems like Las Vegas is prepping Zuhn to be a swing tackle this season.

 

 Round 4 (No. 101): Jermod McCoy , CB. McCoy's first preseason game was rough, allowing two touchdowns. But he has looked much better since, especially in man coverage against the Texans. The Raiders will continue to be patient since McCoy hasn't played football in more than a year due to a knee injur y, but there's confidence that he'll eventually be a reliable outside corner.

 Round 4 (No. 122): Mike Washington Jr ., RB. The Raiders are expected to rely on Washington quite a bit, especially with Ashton Jeanty 's recent ankle injury . Washington's performance this preseason shows he could handle the extended workload.

 Round 5 (No. 150): Dalton Johnson , S. Johnson will be a depth piece in the secondary, with Las Vegas using him as a nickel in practice lately.

 Round 5, (No. 175): Hezekiah Masses , CB. Masses has received a fair number of first-team reps throughout training camp. There is not a ton of veteran experience among the Raiders' cornerbacks, so Masses has an opportunity to make a difference.

 Round 6 (No. 195): Malik Benson , WR. Benson has been a reliable pass catcher for both Kirk Cousins and Mendoza. Will that translate into the regular season? Only time will tell, but Benson has set himself up to get playing time.

 

 Round 7 (No. 229): Brandon Cleveland , DT.  Cleveland might have a tough climb to make the initial 53-man roster and could start the season on the practice squad. -- Ryan McFadden 

 
 

 New York Jets 
 Round 1 (No. 2): David Bailey , Edge. Bailey looks like the real deal . His first-step quickness is exceptional, and he flashes surprising power on his bull rushes. If there's a knock, it's that he needs to show more awareness in run defense. Bailey will start in the base defense and play in several sub packages. "He's everything that we expect him to be," coach Aaron Glenn said.

 Round 1 (No. 16): Kenyon Sadiq , TE. He missed virtually the entire training camp due to a setback from offseason hernia surgery . Sadiq is expected to be ready for Week 1, but the lost time will hurt his ability to make an early impact. When healthy, he's a versatile and explosive player who can line up anywhere, including the backfield. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich will have fun utilizing Sadiq, describing him as "a high-horsepower guy," but it will take a while.

 Round 1 (No. 30): Omar Cooper Jr ., WR. Many assumed Cooper would be the No. 3 receiver behind Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell , but that's not a lock. Cooper lost ground in camp and is now engaged in a battle with Isaiah Williams for that job. Cooper's explosiveness isn't dazzling, and his route running needs refinement. He has lined up mostly on the outside, but he's capable of playing the slot.

 Round 2 (No. 50): D'Angelo Ponds , CB. Ponds was expected to compete for the nickel job, maybe even an outside corner position, but he missed the entire camp with a calf strain. It's fair to wonder if he will be active in Week 1, considering the lost time. It has been a frustrating summer for Ponds.

 Round 4 (No. 103): Darrell Jackson Jr ., DT. Jackson has been a pleasant surprise who has played his way into the defensive line rotation.

 Round 4 (No. 110): Cade Klubnik , QB. He doesn't have the biggest arm, but the organization loves his intangibles, which is a big reason he's the odds-on favorite to be the No. 2 quarterback.

 Round 6 (No. 188): Anez Cooper , G. He went from third team to second team after the first preseason game. Cooper will make the 53 but could be inactive on game day.

 

 Round 7 (No. 228): VJ Payne , S. Payne is expected to return soon from an early-camp injury but will be at the bottom of the 53-man roster if he's not put on the practice squad. -- Rich Cimini 

 
 

 Arizona Cardinals 
 Round 1 (No. 3): Jeremiyah Love , RB. When he was healthy, Love was everything the Cardinals imagined -- fast, quick, strong, a great route runner, great hands. His teammates raved about him and all the facets of his game. When he finally made his debut against the Raiders in the second preseason game, he ended up with a high ankle sprain and hasn't practiced or played since. He won't play again this preseason and might not practice until Week 1.

 

 Round 2 (No. 34): Chase Bisontis , G. Bisontis was put on injured reserve with a torn left MCL that he suffered during the preseason game against the Raiders. Before that, Bisontis was progressing each week, according to coach Mike LaFleur. He was likely going to be a backup but could've been inserted into the starting lineup if needed.

 Round 3 (No. 65): Carson Beck , QB. Beck is dealing with sore ribs after taking a hit during the Hall of Fame Game on Aug. 6 and hasn't practiced or played since. He was making steady growth before then, showing flashes of his arm and touch during training camp. He might be back soon, but his injury stunted his training camp progress.

 Round 4 (No. 104): Kaleb Proctor , DT. Proctor was put on season-ending IR with a torn meniscus that he suffered during OTAs.

 Round 5 (No. 143): Reggie Virgil , WR. Virgil has impressed during training camp and has put in enough good tape to likely make the team as a bottom-of-the-depth-chart receiver.

 Round 6 (No. 183): Karson Sharar , LB. Sharar dealt with injuries during OTAs and minicamp but has recovered and is starting to find his footing.

 

 Round 7 (No. 217): Jayden Williams , OT. Williams worked his way up to the second-team offensive line throughout camp, impressing…

title: First Packers-Cardinals LaFleur matchup: From Michigan brothers to NFL head coaches
summary: No one in the family ever expected it. Now the LaFleurs are the league's newest brother head coaches, with a Lambeau Field reunion set for Friday.
full_text:
DENNY AND KRISTI LaFleur knew their sons, Matt and Mike, would give them a hard time, but they provided a tour of their Green Bay, Wisconsin home anyway.

 As they descended a stairway, both Denny and Kristi warned that Matt would surely not approve.

 "No, don't show them the 'Focker Wall,'" Matt would instruct his parents.

 But, after turning a corner, there, in all its glory, was "The Focker Wall," -- a key focal point in the LaFleur home. The nickname is an homage to a scene from the movie "Meet the Fockers" in which it displays all of Gaylord Focker's accomplishments, from ninth-place ribbons to childhood stuffies.

 The LaFleur family wall, for the record, is a bit more modest.

 There are large portraits of Matt and Mike quarterbacking the teams at Saginaw Valley State and Elmhurst College, respectively.

 "They're going to kill me when I say this, they were Doug Flutie-type quarterbacks," Denny said, grinning, as he described the photos. There are vintage-style Green Bay Packers and Arizona Cardinals signs, and several family photos, mostly featuring their four grandchildren, at NFL stadiums.

 "Terrible," Matt LaFleur said of the wall, and his mom's choice decor. "So brutal," chimes in younger brother, Mike, on a group text thread.

 But Kristi and Denny do not think twice about their sons' decor opinions. They like what they like. They're proud. This is their home. Plus, no amount of good-natured ribbing could disband this group.

 "We're not a very big family," Denny, Kristi, Matt and Mike each echoed, separately. "But we are a tight-knit family."

 

 Matt, 46, and Mike, 39, grew up in Mount Pleasant, Michigan, a town of 24,000 people about 2½ hours northwest of Detroit. A seven-year age gap separates the brothers, along with noticeable personality differences.

 Matt is self-described as a pain in the ass and stubborn, and his family members agree. Mike is known as a bit more easy going.

 "He's probably -- I mean, it's not probably, he is easier to deal with than I am for sure," Matt said, grinning, as the brothers sat together -- bantering and ribbing each other -- at the NFL's annual meetings in March in Phoenix.

 Both take pride in their hair, neither deferring to the other as having the best coif. Though -- spoiler alert! -- their parents might have better hair than either of them.

 Now, the eighth-year coach of the Packers and first-year coach of the Cardinals, Matt and Mike, respectively, are only the fourth brother duo in NFL history to be named head coaches after Jon and Jay Gruden, John and Jim Harbaugh and Al and Ted Nesser.

 On Friday, their families will gather at Denny and Kristi's home -- they relocated nearly four years ago from Michigan -- that sits in the shadow of Lambeau Field, before walking a few minutes to the stadium to watch Matt and Mike face off in a final preseason tuneup ( 8 p.m. ET ) before each of their teams open the 2026 regular season on Sept. 13.

 Raised by parents who were teachers and coaches, it's little surprise that both Matt and Mike forged similar paths.

 But when asked if he could have ever foreseen that one day both he and his younger brother would earn titles as NFL head coaches?

 "I'd say, 'You're full of s---,'" Matt said. "It is pretty surreal."

 
 FOR A FIRST GRADE student, there's hardly a more anticipated decision in the school year than what to bring for show-and-tell.

 For 7-year-old Matt, the decision was easy: his new baby brother, Mikey. So, on a spring morning, Kristi packed up baby Mikey and took him to school for Matt to share with his classmates.

 "He was very, very proud that this is his baby brother," Kristi recalled.

 

 Matt and Mike's age gap spared their parents from some of the rigors of raising two active boys.

 "There was never any shoving, yelling," Kristi said. There was no sibling rivalry. There really weren't any issues at all, except this one time. Matt was pretty irritated with Mikey. Matt was 16, Mikey was 9. Matt said, 'Well, he shows me no respect.'"

 Kristi looked at Matt and started laughing.

 "He's 9," she told him.

 "That is the only thing that I can really remember him ever saying, because they really did not argue," Kristi said. "There was too much age difference there."

 "He was the best," Matt said about Mike. "Just wanted to be around, and he used to get me in trouble all the time because I was the older brother, and he would kind of just needle me a little bit. And of course, I took the bait and would put him in his place, and my parents would always get mad at me saying that I needed to be more mature and accepting of it."

 What would Mike needle him about?

 "I just wanted to hang out," Mike said. "He just didn't want me by. That's all true for sure, and what else is true is he would get the brunt of it from Mom and Dad, particularly Mom."

 Matt and Mike grew up with their dad busy coaching. Denny spent two decades as a Central Michigan football assistant before coaching and teaching at Mount Pleasant High, where Kristi also taught and coached track and cheerleading.

 "Dad was always coaching," Matt said. "[Mom] was there in the morning and she would be the one to, you know, tuck us in to go to bed."

 Matt and Mike spent their days playing outside. Kristi would take them with her to the grocery store, where she would run into what felt like most of the community. Mike was tagging along as Matt went to his various practices. And they spent a lot of time at various football fields rooting for their dad's teams.

 But one of Mike's most memorable moments was with the band.

 

 "He followed the marching band in the stadium and play his little whatever, drums or trombone or whatever it was," Matt said, smiling because this is his favorite story of his little brother.

 "I think I was in the newspaper like at 4 years old playing the -- it wasn't even a drum at one point. It was just like an old coffee tin or something like that because, again, parents were teachers," Mike said.

 Matt interrupted: "We got video of this."

 Kristi gave her boys quote books and instilled in them the power of positive thinking. And even when the boys wouldn't want to hear it, she would keep going, knowing that they were listening.

 "The best coach in the family," Matt said of his mom.

 "She has had a huge influence on how we go about our business," Mike said.

 The dynamic shifted when Matt left to play quarterback at Saginaw Valley State, located about an hour from Mount Pleasant. As a sixth grader, Mike went with his parents to watch his big brother play. A few years later, as a graduate assistant at Central Michigan, Matt repaid the investment and made time to support his little brother.

 
 MATT FACETIMED MIKE , who initially didn't want to pick up because he was busy inside the mobile telephone store.

 But his brother got him to step outside, before breaking the news.

 "I'm like, 'Dude... I got the job!" recalled Matt, who went on to describe seeing Mike on the screen jump up and down and exclaim, "It's the F'ing Packers. The F'ing Packers!"

 The Packers hired LaFleur, after 16 years climbing the coaching ranks, as their head coach in January 2019.

 "That's one moment that I'll always remember that we have together," Matt said.

 For Kristi and Denny, Matt made sure both were sitting down when he delivered the good news.

 "What he said was, 'I got it,' and I thought it was the second interview," Denny recalled. "It's a good thing we sat down, because that just floored us. We were overwhelmed."

 

 Seven years after that video call inside the store, Mike delivered the family his own bit of news.

 "I called him right away," Mike said. "I said, 'We cannot call mom and dad. And he ends up saying, well, when we do tell mom and dad, let's all FaceTime together. And I said, 'Dude, I'm going to FaceTime them. You can stay out of this one for a minute."

 "I just wanted to be a part of this, you know?" Matt quipped.

 When the call came in,…

title: Cardinals' Carson Beck losing valuable reps with setback
summary: With veteran Jacoby Brissett as the starter and Gardner Minshew the backup, Beck will have to make due.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Once the regular season starts, Carson Beck will be in a position familiar to all the quarterbacks around the NFL who aren't starters.

 With how practices are structured during the season, there isn't enough time for the backup and third-string quarterback to get a significant amount of reps. With  Arizona Cardinals  starter Jacoby Brissett set to get the majority of snaps and Gardner Minshew II expected to back up Brissett, Beck should get what's left -- if any -- as the third-stringer.

 It's something Arizona's first-year head coach Mike LaFleur has thought about, but he hasn't divulged his plan for getting Beck more reps once the season starts.

 "I'm not going to dive into it because we don't have to worry about that right now, but it's definitely on the forefront," he said. "I apologize not answering that question right now, because it is valid. And I do think in due time we get closer, I'll answer that for you."

 That made Beck's first NFL training camp all the more important.

 He was getting reps during walk-throughs and practice. Then after a rib injury in the Hall of Fame Game on Aug. 6, he practiced a few days after that until soreness set in and hasn't taken a practice rep in the past couple of weeks.

 It's been a setback for the third-round pick, who was progressing nicely through the first three weeks of training camp.

 "It's easy to magnify the quarterback position and the rookie and all that kind of stuff," LaFleur said. "But yeah, you get better at football by practicing and playing football. And so, when you're not out there, it's hard to get better. So, he's missed some days, but that's no different than the nose guard, that's no different than the receiver, that's no different than the left tackle, particularly for the younger guys.

 "So, it is what it is. I mean, injuries are part of this thing, and he's a tough dude. I mean, he battled through it for three or four practices before the discomfort became so real that it just wasn't worth it because it wasn't going to improve until we gave him a little bit of time."

 LaFleur didn't know whether Beck's prolonged absence in camp will impact how quickly he could get on the field in the regular season, if he were needed.

 "I mean, that's the hypothetical question right now that I couldn't even answer," LaFleur said.

 Beck's return before the season starts doesn't appear likely. LaFleur said it's still to be determined whether Beck will play in Friday night's preseason finale against the  Packers , but Beck didn't participate in Wednesday's joint practice in Green Bay.

 Beck's approach to his first pro training camp wasn't about judging success.

 "I know that's super cliché to say and being process-oriented, but that's what it is," Beck said. "Because again, if they're dropping back in a zone and we have some type of concept and I'm like, 'Ooh, I think I can fit that in there.' Well, now's the time to try. In the game, the checkdown's going to be open if they drop into the zone, but you'll never know if you can make that throw or test through things. And again, it's all trial and error, trial and error. And for me, again, being new in this offense and just continuing to develop as a rookie and as a new guy, I think these learning moments are so huge.

 "But the more reps you get, the more comfortable you become and you kind of start to understand what you're trying to accomplish."

 For Beck, the preseason was supposed to be a slow, steady build toward the regular season. His transition to the NFL was multifaceted. There was the speed of the game, a new offense to learn, new terminology to memorize and new defenses to learn and decipher. The long days of camp, however, weren't new to Beck.

 His training camps at the University of Georgia under Kirby Smart and at the University of Miami under Mario Cristobal, both disciples of the Nick Saban coaching tree, were "just hell." Those camps and the Cardinals' sessions this year were "very similarly structured."

 But the preseason was new to Beck, as it is for all rookies. It's games that don't count and is full of bland offenses and defenses -- "The defense isn't doing anything," LaFleur said. "We're not doing anything." That meant the focus was more on Beck's operation and process, quarterbacks coach Matt Schaub said.

 "The blinders are on," Schaub said.

 He didn't look too far down the line because Beck simply didn't know what he didn't know and it was up to Schaub to teach him. It was a philosophy that Beck embraced.

 In order to improve despite not being results-oriented, Beck also had blinders on.

 "I think the most simple answer is literally to make the most out of every single rep, but it can't be the result that you're looking for," Beck said. "Just because I throw a completion, I'm like, 'Oh, that was a good rep.' But you have no idea. My eyes could have been in the completely wrong spot and the whole, just, coverage was wrong and I got a completion. But if I get the completion, it's like, 'oh, that's a good rep.' No, my eyes were in the wrong spot. If somebody on defense didn't bust, I did the rep totally wrong. You know what I'm saying? So, looking at it from that perspective of, am I doing it right?

 "And then also just getting mental reps when I'm not in. I think that's a huge thing that I learned how to do when I was at Georgia when I sat for three years and then started, and really just trying to take advantage of each rep that we get in practice, even though I might not be physically getting it. The mental sweat when you're behind the play and just making sure that you're locked in each and every play is something that I feel like is really hard to master, but it's something that I got a lot of practice at when I was sitting at Georgia."

title: 2027 NFL mock draft: Reid's preseason first-round predictions
summary: With the college and NFL seasons about to start, Jordan Reid projected the top 32 picks in next year's draft -- including a blockbuster trade.
full_text:
The 2026 college football season starts this weekend with Week 0, and evaluations for the 2027 NFL draft are already underway. Since releasing my way-too-early mock draft in late April, I've been in the film room dissecting tape while also talking to scouts and evaluators around the league to get an idea on how top prospects are trending. So, let's update those first-round projections with another mock draft.

 This is how I see Round 1 playing out right now . Keep in mind that plenty of changes will shake out between now and next April in Washington, D.C. Players will rise and fall on the board, and some might not even remain in the class. And since we don't know the draft order yet, I used current projections from ESPN's Football Power Index for the 1-32.

 With quarterbacks being such a focal point in this class, I've also projected a trade that would uproot the top of this draft at that position. Let's get this started with that blockbuster deal and then get to predictions for all 32 first-round picks.

 Note: Underclassmen are marked with an asterisk. 

 

 

 Projected trade: Browns move up to No. 1 
 Here, the Browns decide to take fate into their own hands, trading both of their first-round picks (Nos. 4 and 32), a 2027 fourth-round pick and their 2028 second-round pick to the Dolphins for the No. 1 selection. Will Cleveland use it to get its franchise quarterback -- and if so, which one?

 
 

 1. Cleveland Browns  (via projected trade with MIA ) 
 Dante Moore , QB, Oregon* 

 I had the Dolphins trade out because they recently invested in Malik Willis . While a lot depends on Willis' performance this season, Miami does already have a promising young quarterback. Unless  Shedeur Sanders  makes a massive leap in Year 2 ( which seems unlikely ), the Browns do not.  Deshaun Watson 's contract ends after this season, as well, making this a perfect time for Cleveland to take another swing at that elusive franchise QB to join the young talent it has accumulated in the past couple drafts.

 Moore has squeaky-clean mechanics, and his accuracy shined in his first year as a starter. This would be a good situation for him, with young players he can grow alongside. If he brings his stellar college play to the NFL, the Browns could turn things around quickly.

 
 

 2. Arizona Cardinals 
 Arch Manning , QB, Texas* 

 Even though Carson Beck , Arizona's third-round pick in April, has looked good this preseason, his presence wouldn't prevent the Cardinals from looking at a QB here -- especially with veteran Jacoby Brissett 's contract expiring after the season. Manning recovered from a slow start to 2025, with his development taking a big leap in mid-October. If he can build on that momentum and improve his accuracy on underneath throws, he has the physical tools to be picked at this spot and join 2026 first-round running back Jeremiyah Love to form Arizona's backfield of the future.

 
 

 3. New York Jets 
 CJ Carr , QB, Notre Dame* 

 The Jets' drafts in the past five years have seen them bring in bookend offensive tackles ( Olu Fashanu and Armand Membou ), a true WR1 ( Garrett Wilson ), a franchise RB ( Breece Hall ) and two talented tight ends ( Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq ). Seems like an ideal base for a young quarterback to join. Carr's sample size is small (12 career starts), but he thrived last season in his first year as a starter. He's a capable passer who can distribute the ball and does a great job of syncing his feet, eyes and throwing motion. Notre Dame is a prime national title contender in 2026, and if Carr excels on that quest, it's easy to see him rise to this spot of the draft.

 

 
 

 4. Miami Dolphins  (via projected trade with CLE ) 
 Jeremiah Smith , WR, Ohio State* 

 The Dolphins fell three spots via our mock trade and would still be able to get my top-ranked player at a severe position of need. Smith grew up down the road from Hard Rock Stadium and would immediately become Miami's go-to receiver. At 6-foot-3, 225 pounds, he is a physically imposing wideout who glides past defenders and is capable of winning with speed or power. He's the best of Ohio State's recent run of first-round receivers. Not only would he be a massive upgrade from  Malik Washington and Jalen Tolbert , but he would also allow Miami to correctly evaluate QB Malik Willis.

 
 

 5. Las Vegas Raiders 
 Cam Coleman , WR, Texas* 

 The Raiders got their QB1 in April when they picked  Fernando Mendoza ; now they get their true WR1. Coleman is a sleek-built pass catcher who can make acrobatic receptions look routine with his outstanding catch radius. He transferred from Auburn to Texas , and this upcoming season could see his production explode as Arch Manning's featured option. Coleman can run every route on the route tree, so having him join 2024 first-rounder Brock Bowers and 2025 first-rounder Ashton Jeanty  would give Las Vegas a formidable core around Mendoza.

 
 

 6. Tennessee Titans 
 Dylan Stewart , Edge, South Carolina* 

 Even though they picked  Keldric Faulk in Round 1 in April, the Titans could use more edge-rush help, especially with Jermaine Johnson II  entering the final year of his contract. Few edge-rush prospects have ever possessed Stewart's blend of upfield acceleration, bend and closing speed. The production has yet to match the potential, as Stewart had only 4.5 sacks last season, but the 6-foot-5, 250-pounder has rare tools and already has teams giddy about what he could develop into at the NFL level.

 
 

 7. Carolina Panthers 
 Leonard Moore , CB, Notre Dame* 

 With  Mike Jackson set to be a free agent who could cash in elsewhere if he repeats his 2025 performance, the Panthers might have a vacancy at cornerback opposite Jaycee Horn . Adding Moore would give Carolina a dynamic coverage duo, as Moore is one of the best corners I've scouted in some time. He has been exceptional at Notre Dame and had five interceptions last season. His length (6-foot-2, 197 pounds) and fluidity give him potential to be a shutdown cover guy.

 
 

 8. New Orleans Saints 
 Colin Simmons , Edge, Texas* 

 The Saints need edge help in both the short term and long term, as  Chase Young and Carl Granderson  will be free agents in 2028. Simmons would be a major boost to New Orleans' defensive front as the most productive edge rusher in this class. He led the SEC with 12 sacks last season, and the 6-foot-3, 245-pounder is a terror with an unpredictable assortment of pass-rush moves. His combination of power and upfield quickness has him in the argument with Dylan Stewart as the top edge in this draft.

 

 
 

 9. New York Giants 
 Will Echoles , DT, Ole Miss* 

 The Giants traded away star defensive tackle  Dexter Lawrence II  this offseason, creating a gaping hole in their defensive interior. Echoles is the best of a deep defensive tackle crop, as his power and pass-rush push give him a well-rounded skill set. The 6-foot-3, 315-pound Echoles is a stout run defender who is difficult to move off the spot, allowing him to maintain gap control and generate negative plays. He just turned 20 years old earlier this month, giving him tremendous room for growth.

 
 

 10. Washington Commanders 
 Charlie Becker , WR, Indiana* 

 Even though  Stefon Diggs just signed with Washington , he'll be 33 years old and it's unclear if he'll be the Commanders' WR2 past this season. There's still a need for help opposite Terry McLaurin , and the 6-foot-4, 207-pound Becker was the player I enjoyed studying the most this offseason. He exploded on the scene last November and was the X factor in Indiana's run to the national title , averaging 19.9 yards per reception (seventh in the FBS). Becker combines deep speed with elite ball tracking and excellent hand-eye coordination. His skill set would perfectly complement Jayden Daniels ' deep-ball proficiency.

 
 

 11. Atlanta Falcons 
 Trevor Goosby , OT, Texas*

title: 2026 NFL offseason trade grades: Tutu Atwell, Kayshon Boutte
summary: We're making sense of a few big preseason deals, including the Tutu Atwell to the Rams and Kayshon Boutte to the Texans.
full_text:
The main transaction window of the 2026 NFL offseason is over, with free agency and the draft long behind us. But teams are still leaning on trades to improve their rosters between now and Week 1. And we're grading the biggest swaps around the league, putting each deal into perspective for teams.

 The post-June 1 deals started with a bang. The Browns are  trading  edge rusher  Myles Garrett to the Rams for multiple draft picks -- including a 2027 first-rounder -- and edge rusher Jared Verse . The Patriots finally made their move to bring in Eagles wide receiver  A.J. Brown , giving up two draft picks. Did the Rams overpay in a massive return for Cleveland? Does Brown complete New England's offense? And how do we feel about the Falcons acquiring offensive tackle Wanya Morris , the Texans getting wide receiver  Kayshon Boutte  and the Rams bringing back  wide receiver  Tutu Atwell ?

 To determine each grade, I am looking at multiple factors, including on-field impact, salary cap implications, compensation, player value/age and the context of a team's short- and long-term outlooks. How large is the effect of this decision, and how sure are we that it's a good or bad choice? How does this affect a team's chance to win the Super Bowl, this season or in the future?

 Let's get into our grades, and check back throughout training camp and the preseason for more trade evaluations.

 
 See more: 
 Tracking trades over the summer 
 Grades from earlier in the offseason 

 
 

 

 Dolphins trade WR Atwell to Rams 
 Date: Aug. 27 

 Rams get: WR Tutu Atwell 
 Dolphins get: RB Jarquez Hunter 

 Rams grade: B 
 Dolphins grade: B

 It's safe to say that no team likes Atwell as much as the Rams. A year ago, the Rams re-signed him to a one-year, $10 million deal that raised eyebrows at the time (and still does now). Atwell was coming off a season in which he recorded 562 receiving yards but had done so on 2.2 yards per route run. But the $10 million wasn't worth it -- he ran a route on just 35% of Rams dropbacks last season and amassed only 192 receiving yards (1.4 yards per route run).

 

 The Rams let him walk in free agency, with the Dolphins signing him to a one-year, $1.4 million contract . But apparently Atwell could not hang in Miami, even against a weak receiving group that included Malik Washington , Jalen Tolbert and several rookies, such as third-rounders Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell .

 The fact the Rams are bringing him back is telling about how they feel about their receiver depth. After Puka Nacua and Davante Adams , the depth chart is awfully lackluster, with Jordan Whittington , Konata Mumpfield , Xavier Smith and rookie  CJ Daniels . The Rams play a lot of tight ends -- they played 13 personnel (one RB, three TEs) more than twice as much any other team last season -- but there will still be snaps when they need three wide receivers on the field. And there's no guarantee Nacua and Adams are available all season.

 Hunter was a 2025 fourth-round pick who not only failed to surpass Blake Corum for the backup running back role last season but didn't record a single carry. He'll battle with Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II for a depth position in Miami.

 If both players were on the roster bubble of their respective teams, it makes sense to swap them for similar players at positions where more depth is needed.

 

 

 Patriots trade WR Boutte to Texans 
 Date: Aug. 24

 Texans get: WR Kayshon Boutte 
 Patriots get: S Jaylen Reed , 2028 seventh-round pick

 Texans grade: A 
 Patriots grade: C

 Jayden Higgins ' season-ending torn ACL created a major need for the Texans. Houston had to add an outside wide receiver who could produce opposite Nico Collins , particularly one who could execute Higgins' route profile. They found a pretty ideal replacement in Boutte -- a short-term solution available for cheap, but one who should step in and help right away.

 Higgins ran a go route or deep fade on 18% of his routes last season, the 10th-highest rate among all receivers with at least 300 routes run. Boutte was No. 1 in that category by a mile at 31%, so he should have no problem assuming those deep routes along with slants, a route both Higgins and Boutte ran frequently last season.

 While not a star, Boutte is solid at what he does. He recorded 1.6 yards per route run during a mini-breakout season in 2025. Having a receiver with his route tree gives Collins help while allowing Houston to see how Jaylin Noel develops and how Tank Dell recovers from injury without them having to be impact players right away. Getting Boutte at this point of the offseason for as little as they did is good business.

 I can understand why the Patriots made Boutte available -- he had been bumped down the depth chart after the team had acquired both A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason -- but that doesn't he should have been, at least for this price. The Patriots are trying to win now and having a deep receiving group for Drake Maye to throw to seems like a worthwhile endeavor. New England's ticket back to the Super Bowl is through an elite passing game. And even if Boutte had left in free agency in a year, there's a chance the Patriots could have earned a compensatory pick in exchange.

 In addition to the future draft pick, the Patriots acquired Reed, a 2025 sixth-round pick. Reed played 73 defensive snaps in seven games last season, aligning as a box safety or nickel roughly two-thirds of the time. He should provide depth for the Patriots.

 

 

 Chiefs trade OT Morris to Falcons 
 Date: June 11

 Falcons get: OT Wanya Morris , 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Chiefs get: 2027 sixth-round pick

 Falcons grade: B+ 
 Chiefs grade: B-

 Two days after the Chiefs decided to explore trade options for Morris, who was hoping for a better path to playing time, they found a partner. Coincidentally, Morris will likely find himself competing for playing time with former Chiefs teammate  Jawaan Taylor  in Atlanta.

 

 A 2023 third-round pick, Morris played only 1,085 snaps and started 16 games over three seasons with the Chiefs, including one start in 2025 before suffering a season-ending knee injury on the opening snap of that game.

 His numbers have been solid when he's on the field, though. Morris has a career 89.3% pass block win rate and 73.5% run block win rate at tackle, which are both a shade below average for a starter. That said, win rates for Chiefs players have often been a bit better than expected, so those figures should come with a small grain of salt. And he had recently fallen down the depth chart, according to ESPN's Nate Taylor .

 The Falcons have veteran Jake Matthews entrenched at left tackle. But Jawaan Taylor is atop the depth chart at right tackle after his disappointing tenure in Kansas City as the Falcons try to fill the void from Kaleb McGary's retirement . Taylor signed a one-year, $5 million deal with Atlanta this offseason, which suggests that he's not entrenched as the starter -- especially since he's missed OTAs for undisclosed reasons . Morris is on the final year of his rookie contract.

 With Morris gone, the Chiefs suddenly lack proven depth at tackle, and coach Andy Reid has said the right tackle spot is a competition rather than  Jaylon Moore 's job to lose.

 

 

 Eagles trade WR Brown to the Patriots 
 Date: June 1

 Patriots get:  WR  A.J. Brown 
 Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 first-round pick

 Patriots grade: B- 
 Eagles grade: A-

 The inevitable trade finally happened: Brown is headed to the Patriots. With the Eagles and Brown long headed for a split, the wide receiver is reuniting with his old head coach, Mike Vrabel. The hope is clear that Brown can augment an already-strong passing offense with Drake Maye at the helm to give New England a good shot to get back to the Super Bowl.

 I have long been bullish on Brown relative to consensus. Even though he has widely been considered one of the better NFL receivers over the past six…

title: NFL Rivalries uniforms 2026: Designs, debuts and details
summary: The second iteration of the NFL's Rivalries uniform series is unveiled with eight new teams from the AFC South and NFC North sharing their threads.
full_text:
Eight new squads unveiled their threads on Tuesday for the second edition of the NFL's Rivalries uniform series.

 

 The AFC South and NFC North teams will each wear special uniforms for a home game against a division rival. The Indianapolis Colts will be the first team to debut a Rivalries uniform this campaign when they face the Houston Texans in Week 3. The Chicago Bears are the last to do so in Week 16 against the Green Bay Packers . 

 Last season, teams from the AFC East and NFC West rang in the new initiative, which the league says is meant to celebrate rivalries in the NFL. Each design is created in collaboration with the team, Nike and the league. 

 The uniforms will remain in each team's rotation for three years alongside its existing alternate looks. The NFC East and AFC West squads will unveil theirs next season, and the NFC South and AFC North round out the first batch in 2028. NFC West and AFC East teams will continue to wear their designs this season.

 Here's a breakdown of each uniform design, plus the date of its on-field debut, its unique name and quotes from select teams.

 

 Chicago Bears 
 One of the oldest squads in the NFL, Chicago leans into that rich history in a modern way with a look that pays homage to founder George Halas' legacy and the team's "historic resilience." A patch honoring Halas appears on the front of the jersey, similar to what the team wore in 1983 after his death.

 The Bears' burnt orange and deep blue colorway is a classic. The vertical stripe detail on the sleeves is a reinterpretation of a staple design element, and the four stars of the city's flag are referenced on it. Chicago first wore orange pants in the 1930s, and it will return with classic-modern detailing for this design. "Monsters of the Midway" runs on the back of the neckline.

 On-field debut:  Week 16 vs. Green Bay Packers

 

 

 Detroit Lions 
 Detroit is looking forward to the future while highlighting the city's legacy as "a hub for innovation."

 The primary white uniform includes Honolulu blue scattered throughout, a key color in the Lions' palette. Of course, there are elements to the city's car and racing culture -- the sleek carbon-fiber-italicized numerals -- as well as the "Defend the Den" mentality, with a shoulder-pad pattern mimicking a lion's gaze. "Defend the Den" also appears on the back neckline.

 On-field debut: Week 8 vs. Minnesota Vikings 

 

 

 Green Bay Packers 
 The Packers have been a publicly owned, nonprofit corporation since 1923 with just over 530,000 stockholders. It creates a different bond with the fans, one that the new uniform taps into on various levels.

 The design is meant to honor the unique tradition and Vince Lombardi-era legacy in a fresh look for fans. A retro-style "GB" logo appears on the front. Green Bay's uniform includes a "vintage, desaturated green" paired with an "alabaster palette." It pays homage to the Packers' six stock sales over 107 years: 1923, 1935, 1950, 1997, 2011 and 2022. "Making history since 1919" appears on the back of the uniform neck.

 On-field debut:  Week 5 vs. Chicago Bears

 

 

 Houston Texans 
 Houston's look refreshes its H-Town identity inspired by three elements: car culture, street art and local texture.

 It's an all-white design with metallic finishes and chrome details that connect to the city's automobile scene. The blue number set is inspired by Houston's "Be Someone" bridge, which was anonymously painted in 2012 on the city's I-10 and I-45 bridge. "Houston" runs on the back of the uniform with "US" bolded in a blue, similar to the number set.

 On-field debut:  Week 11 vs. Indianapolis Colts

 

 

 Indianapolis Colts 
 Indianapolis' uniform includes classic elements of the team's typical design with twists.

 The team's signature two-stripe design is a key part of it in a dark blue on the shoulder sleeve with black accents. Anthracite, dark gray and glossy black elements run through the uniform adding "depth and intensity." Different references to the Colts' horseshoe (shoulder sleeve), ironwork and pregame anvil ritual nail home the team tradition. On the back neckline is "For the Shoe."

 On-field debut:  Week 3 vs. Houston Texans

 

 

 Jacksonville Jaguars 
 There are various inspirations for the Jaguars' design, but the most prominent is a simple one: the beach.

 Florida's coastal culture and urban influence shape the color, a clean cream that pops. What the team describes as a "historically influenced" custom Jaguars script appears across the chest. There's a distinct drop shadow around the number set plus Jaguar-print pant details. "Bold City" is on the back neckline, and the Jaguars' logo runs on the sleeve near metallic chrome accents.

 On-field debut:   Week 8 vs. Indianapolis Colts

 

 

 Minnesota Vikings 
 It's a different purple than what the team usually wears, described as a "deeper, more intimidating" one. There's an ivory palette with carved number details, and the "Vikings" above the numbers has a unique font. On the sleeve is a refined cap inspired by the Viking Knot for a neat design.

 There are also references to the Gjallarhorn, which according to Norse mythology is used to sound the arrival of the gods. It is blown before the Vikings take the field at home. Similar to the other teams, Minnesota has a message on the back of its uniform. But the Vikings' message is in the runes script.

 On-field debut:  Week 15 vs. Detroit Lions

 

 

 Tennessee Titans 
 Tennessee has a rich history of star musicians, from Dolly Parton to Elvis Presley to Justin Timberlake, among many other greats. And with the Titans playing in Nashville, it's no surprise they leaned into the "Music City" moniker for their design.

 It's a navy uniform with light blue accents around the "Music City" above the similarly colored numbers. Nashville's famous neon signage inspires the light blue number set. On the shoulder of the uniform are six darker blue strings, meant to celebrate the city's music culture. "WE" runs on the back neckline.

 On-field debut:  Week 10 vs. Jacksonville Jaguars

title: Is Vikings rookie Caleb Banks healthy and ready to perform?
summary: It appears Banks is over his foot surgeries, but questions linger about the first-rounder's conditioning.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The biggest question facing the Minnesota Vikings ' top draft pick this summer was clear: Is defensive lineman Caleb Banks healthy after undergoing three surgeries to repair a broken left foot?

 The answer has been a clear affirmative. Banks has missed only one practice, and that was a planned rest day, while playing 47 defensive snaps in the first two preseason games. 

 Which brings us to the second-biggest question: Can he play at the level the Vikings projected when they made him the No. 18 selection of the 2026 draft?

 That answer is less obvious.

 The consensus after watching Banks move through his first training camp is that he is not yet ready to dominate NFL offensive lines. Opponents have found ways to get lower position on his 6-foot-6 frame and push him backwards, and Banks himself acknowledged last weekend that "I'm definitely not in shape" after missing most of his final college season and all of the Vikings' spring practices because of the foot injury. 

 At the very least, however, Banks appears to have joined nose tackle Domonique Orange -- a third-round draft pick -- in earning a regular spot in the Vikings' initial defensive line rotation. 

 "The one thing about [Banks] is he works and it's important to him," defensive coordinator Brian Flores said. "And in my experience, guys who work at it and continually try to improve, they improve and develop."

 

 Banks was one of the more intriguing draft decisions in the NFL this spring. Under the leadership of interim general manager Rob Brzezinski, the Vikings had Banks ranked among the top 10 prospects in the draft. Some people in the organization mentioned him in the context of a long line of Hall of Fame-level defensive linemen in franchise history, from the Purple People Eaters to John Randle to Kevin Williams . But after the foot injury limited him to four games in his final season at Florida and then resurfaced at the NFL combine with another fracture, Banks' draft value grew less certain .

 The Vikings' medical staff examined his foot during a predraft visit and emerged confident that it would fully heal in time for the season. That projection has proved accurate, but the residual loss of conditioning has been obvious to all. Banks joked after Saturday's  13-3 preseason loss to the Baltimore Ravens that he needed to start running more post-practice gassers.

 Flores concurred with that assessment, but believes it puts Banks in a category with many other players.

 

 "He's right that he may not feel like he's in the best of condition," Flores said, "but I'm not sure he really even knows what that looks like, just like any other rookie. And I don't blame him for that. It's something he's going to have to learn on the fly. He's gotten a little bit of a feel for it in these preseason games, what the first half looks like, what starting the third quarter looks like.

 "With these rookies, there's no way for them to step in and think that they're going to have the experience to really know what NFL football's like. But I would say our group's doing a good job. Our coaches are doing a really good job of trying to get them prepared and as ready to go as we possibly can, knowing that we can't mimic what an NFL game is like. And so I think he's right to feel like, 'Hey, I'm not where I need to be.' And I don't think he'll really know until we're really in it."

 Judging Banks' play as the season begins will require the recent context of Flores' scheme, which has often asked defensive linemen to focus on assignments that don't result in splash plays .

 

 Banks did some gentle freelancing in the 13-10 preseason win against the New York Giants  on Aug. 15. After recognizing that he was not going to be double teamed, he used a swim move to get past guard Francis Mauigoa and into the backfield as the Giants handed the ball to running back Cam Skattebo . But Banks missed the tackle, later saying that Skattebo was "faster than I expected," and the play went for 7 yards on first down. 

 Asked about that decision this week, Flores smiled. He made clear that he wants players to have an "element of freedom" and to experiment in training camp and the preseason, in part to learn the value of carrying out the original assignments.

 "That's part of the learning process though," Flores said. "And I ask those guys to try to jump inside. See if you can get there or take the edge. But if you're [past] the quarterback, now you've learned that you probably shouldn't do that. Or you jump inside and they get outside of you, now you've learned. It's like a little kid with a hot stove. He doesn't know it burns until it burns. But that's what training camp is for. That's what preseason's for."

title: 2026 Seattle Seahawks training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Seahawks training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Seattle Seahawks ' camp is taking place in Renton, Washington, and Seahawks reporter Brady Henderson has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Seahawks camp. What is new with the defending Super Bowl champions? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Seahawks camp 
 
 NFL owners approve Seahawks sale to Khosla group 
 Leonard Williams lands 3-year, $90M extension 
 Clark, Richman put on season-ending injured reserve 
 CB Trevon Diggs signing 1-year deal with Seahawks 
 Sources: Seahawks still plan on signing Terrion Arnold 
 Cooper Kupp's latest route? Opening a new coffee shop 
 Seahawks, Witherspoon reach extension: 4 years, $132M, sources say 
 Seahawks' DeMarcus Lawrence confirms 2026 season his last 
 Facing charges, Terrion Arnold set to join Seahawks 
 Seattle's Nick Emmanwori has ankle surgery, expected to play W1 
 Who are the Khoslas? Meet the family set to buy the Seahawks 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 27 
 Just like last year, Seattle's third preseason game will be Jalen Milroe 's to start and finish.

 Coach Mike Macdonald said Thursday that Seahawks starters who did not play in the first two preseason games will again sit Friday against the  Chiefs  in Kansas City. No. 2 quarterback Drew Lock will be ready just in case, Macdonald said, but the plan is for Milroe to play the whole game.

 As a third-round pick last year, Milroe's roster spot is almost certainly secured. But it'll be a chance for Seattle's QB3 to end what has been an underwhelming preseason on a high note. Over the first two games, Milroe has gone 11 of 19 for 88 yards with no touchdowns and a pair of interceptions that both came last week against Tennessee. In each game, he has committed the regrettable error of taking a sack on fourth down. On the positive side, Milroe has shown flashes with his legs, rushing six times for 52 yards. Seahawks coaches have encouraged him to run more this summer and use what Macdonald has called his trump card.

 After all, that was a primary reason Seattle drafted him in the third round with a plan to take advantage of his athleticism in specialty packages early on as he developed as a passer. But when Milroe lost three fumbles while playing the entirety of the third preseason game, it might have marked the beginning of the end of his chances to get regular snaps as a rookie. 

 With Lock still appearing to be in control of the No. 2 job, Friday's preseason finale might mean more for Milroe's long-term development than his chances of getting on the field in 2026.

 "I think it's really great that he has an opportunity, just like the Green Bay game last year, where you're not subbing in, you're not coming in at halftime," Macdonald said. "You're going through the whole process of starting a game and getting in rhythm and managing the situations, all those things that we want from our quarterback. I'm excited to see him play. It's a great opportunity for him."

 More observations: 

 
 Macdonald declined to discuss injury specifics, as he usually does leading up to the regular season, but he did say that the undisclosed injury that has sidelined wide receiver  Tory Horton for the past two weeks is not a long-term concern. 
 Macdonald confirmed that rookie running back  Jadarian Price is among the players who will not play Friday. 
 Cornerback  Trevon Diggs will "get some run" against the Chiefs, Macdonald said. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 26 
 What has Jake Bobo meant to Seattle's wide receiver corps?

 The fourth episode of HBO's "Hard Knocks," which aired Tuesday, painted a colorful picture.

 In the opening scene, Seahawks receivers coach Frisman Jackson is giving Bobo a pep talk in the group's meeting room. He likens Bobo to a pitbull and tells him he's their version of Dennis Rodman, Udonis Haslem and Draymond Green -- NBA bad boys who were/are tasked with protecting the star players and doing things that don't show up in the stat sheet.

 "Your identity is that you're the goon, you're the enforcer," Jackson tells Bobo. "That dude is the f---er that we expect to see all the time: physical, a good in the run game, we throw you a ball, you make a play. That's it."

 The Seahawks will be without those attributes now that Bobo is out for the season because of a torn ACL he sustained last Friday in Seattle's joint practice against the  Tennessee Titans . The injury was a main storyline on "Hard Knocks," with one clip showing coach Mike Macdonald lamenting how his decision to sit a sore Cooper Kupp that day out of precaution meant that Bobo took more reps than usual.

 "That's an absolutely awful situation," Kupp said Wednesday, "and obviously everybody here feels for Jake."

 With Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Kupp and Rashid Shaheed , the Seahawks have as good a receiver trio as any in the NFL. The depth of that group was also supposed to be a strength, but Bobo is now out for the year and Tory Horton -- the projected No. 4 -- continues to deal with an undisclosed injury. It does not appear to be related to the leg fracture that cut Horton's rookie season short and required surgery, but it has been enough to sideline him for nearly two weeks, as Horton was again not on the practice field as warmups began Wednesday.

 Macdonald has not publicly disclosed what Horton is dealing with, only saying Friday that he's "still working through his stuff" and will be "out for a period of time."

 The Seahawks should be OK if Horton is sidelined into the regular season as long as their primary speed threat, Shaheed, remains healthy. But with Bobo not coming back, Seattle's receiver corps will miss its enforcer -- both on the field and off of it.

 "We're a group of men that come together every day to pursue a goal and have our own lives that all coalesce into this story that makes the season come alive," Kupp said. "Not having him be a part of that story moving forward for this year is tough. It's hard. I know he's going to get after things in terms of rehab and all that stuff, but not having Bobo the person around us is going to be tough."

 More observations: 

 
 Among those who were again not in uniform at the start of practice Wednesday were S Nick Emmanwori , TE AJ Barner , RB Emanuel Wilson , RG Anthony Bradford and OT Josh Jones (at this point of camp, reporters are only allowed to watch the warmup period of practice). 
 ESPN has obtained more details of CB Trevon Diggs ' one-year, $1.215 million contract with Seattle. According to a source, the deal has no guaranteed money, but it does include $2 million in incentives. Diggs would earn $500,000 for playing 42% of the defensive snaps, $750,000 for 50%, or $1 million for 60%. He'd earn $500,000 for three interceptions, $750,000 for five interceptions, or $1 million for seven interceptions. 
 

 

 Friday, Aug. 21 

 The Seahawks spent a second-round pick on safety Bud Clark after losing Coby Bryant in free agency, but don't pencil the rookie into the starting lineup just yet. Ty Okada doesn't look like he's giving up that job any time soon.

 "We love Ty," linebacker Ernest Jones IV said Friday after Okada provided a highlight of Seattle's joint practice against the Tennessee Titans . "I think where Ty has grown is that he's just more in command in his voice and speaking up when things aren't right. title: Titans still high on Carnell Tate despite lack of preseason production
summary: Tennessee still believes Carnell Tate will be the playmaker it envisioned after making him the No. 4 pick in April.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- After making a big splash when he first stepped onto the field in OTAs, things have been relatively quiet during the last couple of weeks for Tennessee Titans rookie receiver Carnell Tate . 

 He had carried that initial momentum into minicamp and the start of training camp, but he didn't record a catch in two preseason games on five targets after playing a total of 35 snaps with the starting offense.

 That's hardly the statistical start anyone wanted, but Tate still remains highly regarded by the coaching staff. And they still feel he will be a top playmaker in their offense.

 "I have a great amount of confidence in Tate and how he goes about his business, what he does on the practice field," offensive coordinator Brian Daboll said Tuesday. "Look, I think everybody would love to have 15 catches. But he's doing the right stuff. He's in a good headspace. He's where he's supposed to be."

 

 Tate said he understands the ball isn't always going to find everybody and isn't letting the lack of production over a few preseason games frustrate him.

 "Not every day is going to be your best day and not every game is going to be your best game," Tate said. "I'm just staying levelheaded, going out to compete each and every day. You just got to know how to play with emotion, not let emotion play with you. That's the biggest thing. I just stay calm. Don't get too high. Don't get too low."

 Titans receivers coach Greg Lewis challenges his receivers to know all the pass catching spots in the offense. This way they're interchangeable and get a better understanding of the full passing concept on each play. Despite being a rookie, Tate has been able to pick up the concepts and execute accordingly.

 Lewis called Tate one of the best rookies he's worked with coming from college to the NFL. He praised Tate for the mature way he carries himself, specifically the study habits and how well he's able to implement what he learns on the field.

 Moving across the formation is nothing new for Tate, who noted how as a freshman at Ohio State he had to move to the slot when Emeka Egbuka suffered an ankle injury. Tate also played multiple spots as a sophomore to create mismatches for himself and teammate Jeremiah Smith. This also helped him post 51 receptions for 875 yards and nine touchdowns in his final season.

 Now Tate will be moving around to help create favorable matchups for himself and veteran wideouts  Wan'Dale Robinson  and Calvin Ridley . Having them in the room has also helped Tate digest the playbook. Both Robinson and Ridley have played for Daboll in the past. Robinson with the New York Giants and Ridley at Alabama.

 "I'm leaning on guys that have been around guys that have been around [Daboll]," Tate said. "I pick up and learn as much as possible from Wan'Dale because he's played every position in the offense and has been with [Daboll] for the past four years. And [Ridley] is familiar with the offense as well."

 One of Tate's best plays this summer came from the slot, when he made a leaping catch down the field during a team period as the Titans prepared for joint practice with the  Seattle Seahawks . Tate collided with safety Kevin Winston Jr . but managed to hold onto the pass from Cam Ward despite the contact. He didn't return to practice that day but was on the field when the Titans returned to practice two days later.

 That explosive play is exactly what the Titans were thirsty for when they made him the No. 4 overall pick in April after seeing him catch five touchdowns of 40 yards or more during his career at Ohio State. Various draft analysts lauded Tate for his polished route-running, natural hands-catching ability and fantastic body control while calling him an immediate impact player.

 

 Lewis said he feels Tate has all the skills to be an impactful player. But he challenged Tate to play with more violence as a receiver "every single day, on every single rep, in every single opportunity, whether it's a drill, meeting or any game situation."

 Tate showed some of that in a joint practice against the  Chicago Bears  on Thursday, hauling in two touchdowns from Ward, who targeted him12 times with seven of them resulting in completions. Tate said he's continuing to build on his connection with Ward and he has stayed ready for the ball to come his way.

 "He wants the ball," Ward said. "So when it comes his way, he's urgent to it. He goes up and high points it. He's been great and may not have the splash plays as of late, but he's going to be a key reason why we have success on offense. No. 14 is going to be a playmaker for sure."

 Tennessee now heads into its preseason finale Saturday ( 6 p.m. ET, NFL Network ) against the Bears with Ward giving praise to the way Tate aggressively attacks the football, and despite things not clicking yet on game days, it's that aggression in other moments (like Thursday) that have made Ward still go to Tate. 

 "He's got a dog mentality," Lewis said of Tate. "You ain't going to see it. You just see him go out there and dice you up, not say anything and then come back and do it again."
